stem: 39 y.o with mycoplasma pneumonia started on antibiotics and supportive therapy. On day 3 She started complaining of yellowish discolouration of the eyes and mild abdominal pain Hb 60, Reticulocyte 4 (high) ALT normal AST high Haptoglobin 0.4
key_concept:
Hemolysis after a new drug versus after an infection.
  • Hemolysis markers: low Hb, high reticulocytes, low haptoglobin, high LDH, high indirect bilirubin, AST up more than ALT (released from RBCs).
  • Mycoplasma or EBV: IgM cold agglutinins, usually transient; supportive care, avoid cold.
  • Drug-induced immune hemolysis: stop the drug.
  • Warm AIHA (SLE, CLL, idiopathic): corticosteroids first, rituximab if refractory.
  • Primary cold agglutinin disease: rituximab based therapy; steroids work poorly.
exam_pearl: Mycoplasma plus hemolysis = cold agglutinins, not antibiotic toxicity; the key decision is whether the exam wants supportive care or steroids.
compiler_note:
⚠ Image audit: The compiler marked this answer tentatively ('??' / 'not sure' / needs re-correction) — see the compiler note.
Compiler note: Reference: Harrison's and UpToDate. Mycoplasma pneumonia is a classic cause of cold agglutinin autoimmune hemolytic anemia (IgM cold agglutinins destroy RBCs). Treat the underlying infection; if hemolysis is clinically significant (Hb 60) give corticosteroids. Stopping antibiotics is not the answer: hemolysis is due to Mycoplasma, not the antibiotic. Hemolysis after starting a drug = stop drug; with Mycoplasma = cold agglutinin AIHA = steroids if severe.
Other marked answers: Query marks on B. Stop ABx ??

stem: Pt admitted to hospital and put on medications. after 3 days of admission she developed fatigue, abd pain, yellowish in eyes. Labs: Hb: 68 (normal above 120) Reticulocytes: 4 % Haptoglobin: low LDH: high (Was 300, And 600 in other Recalls). What is the best medication to give?
why_right: Hb 68, reticulocytes 4%, low haptoglobin, rising LDH and jaundice mean acute hemolysis, and it started 3 days after admission and new medications. That timing points to drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia, whose first and most important treatment is stopping the offending drug (here the antibiotic). Most cases settle once the drug is withdrawn.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aspirin has no role in hemolysis; it is a recognised hemolysis trigger in G6PD deficiency and adds bleeding risk.
B. Rituximab is for refractory warm AIHA or primary cold agglutinin disease, not first-line for hemolysis caused by a drug that can simply be stopped.
C. Corticosteroids are first line for warm autoimmune hemolysis (idiopathic, SLE, CLL); in drug-induced hemolysis they are at most an adjunct after the drug is stopped.
key_concept:
New hemolysis after starting a drug: stop the drug first.
  • Hemolysis: low Hb, high reticulocytes, low haptoglobin, high LDH, indirect hyperbilirubinemia.
  • Common culprits: cephalosporins (ceftriaxone), penicillins, NSAIDs.
  • Confirm with direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test.
  • Warm AIHA: steroids, then rituximab if refractory.
  • Severe anemia: transfuse while removing the cause.
exam_pearl: If the hemolysis follows a new drug, removing the trigger beats any added medication; if it follows Mycoplasma, think cold agglutinins instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Harrison's: drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia, management is immediate discontinuation of the causative drug. UpToDate: first step in suspected drug-induced hemolysis is stop the offending medication. Acute hemolysis: Hb 68 very low, reticulocytes 4% marrow responding, low haptoglobin, high LDH (released from destroyed RBCs), jaundice from indirect bilirubin.

stem: A 62-year-old male with a history of uncontrolled hypertension, presented with severe headache and altered mentation. A CT scan of the brain shows an intracerebral hemorrhage. The patient is hemodynamically stable. What is the target of blood pressure acceptable?
key_concept:
ICH blood pressure: lower systolic BP early, but not too far.
  • Hemorrhagic stroke: target SBP about 140 (older teaching: below 140/90).
  • Current AHA guidance: aim for about 140 and keep SBP roughly in the 130 to 150 range; driving it below 130 is linked to harm.
  • Ischemic stroke, no thrombolysis: treat only if above 220/120.
  • Ischemic stroke before/after tPA: keep below 185/110 (then below 180/105).
  • Agents: IV labetalol or nicardipine; smooth, sustained control.
exam_pearl: Uncontrolled hypertension plus severe headache and confusion with ICH on CT is a hypertensive bleed: lower SBP to about 140 smoothly, but avoid overshooting below 130.

⚠ Image audit: Page (top of p82) says 'Answer: C or B'; no single endorsed answer. Card has C.
Compiler note: Answer line: 'C or B'.
Other marked answers: Answer line: B. 120-140 mmHg

stem: A patient came with pneumonia sx productive cough, fever, pain, pic was provided (lobar pneumonia), treatment was initiated (IV cetriaxone, paracetamol, tramadol), after one day he became stable and improved what drug to stop? Reduced platelets count (around 70 I think)
why_right: The new problem is thrombocytopenia (platelets about 70) appearing after treatment was started, in a patient whose pneumonia is otherwise improving. Among the drugs actually given, ceftriaxone is the recognized cause of drug induced immune thrombocytopenia (drug dependent antibodies destroy platelets), so it is the drug to stop. Because he is now stable, the antibiotic can be switched to an appropriate non beta lactam or oral alternative to complete the course.
why_wrong_block:
A. Paracetamol: thrombocytopenia is extremely rare; it is a safe antipyretic and analgesic and would only be stopped for hepatotoxicity concerns.
B. Tramadol: its adverse effects are mainly CNS (sedation, seizures, serotonin syndrome) and nausea, not platelet destruction.
D. Vancomycin: it can cause immune thrombocytopenia, but it was never given to this patient, so it cannot be the culprit.
key_concept:
New cytopenia after starting drugs: identify the most likely culprit among drugs ACTUALLY given and stop it.
  • Drug induced immune thrombocytopenia: platelets fall typically 1 to 2 weeks after first exposure, sooner on re-exposure
  • Common culprits: beta lactams (cephalosporins, penicillins), vancomycin, heparin, quinine, sulfonamides, valproate
  • Management: stop the drug; platelets usually recover within days
  • On heparin: think HIT (4T score) instead
exam_pearl: Read the option list against the drugs given: vancomycin is a real cause but a trap here because it was never started.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0114).

stem: 30-year-old male presented with polydipsia and polyuria, has positive family history of type1 diabetes mellitus; labs show HbA1c 8.5%, C-peptide 0.09 (low), high parathyroid hormone (PTH), high calcium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
OptD: Maturity onset diabetes of the young MOD
highlight_terms_source: positive family history of type1 diabetes mellitus
why_right: HbA1c 8.5% confirms diabetes, and a very low C-peptide means little or no endogenous insulin, which defines type 1 diabetes (adults can develop it, including slow-onset autoimmune LADA). The family history of type 1 DM supports this. High PTH with high calcium is primary hyperparathyroidism, a separate finding that does not change the diabetes diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Type 2 DM is insulin resistance with normal or high C-peptide, typically in older or obese patients; very low C-peptide argues against it.
C. Central DI causes polyuria and polydipsia with dilute urine and high serum sodium/osmolality, but HbA1c would be normal; here hyperglycemia explains the symptoms.
D. MODY is an autosomal dominant monogenic diabetes in young patients with several affected generations and preserved C-peptide, usually autoantibody negative; fits poorly with absent insulin secretion.
key_concept:
C-peptide separates insulin deficiency from insulin resistance.
  • Low C-peptide: type 1 DM (or LADA in adults).
  • Normal/high C-peptide: type 2 DM or MODY.
  • Islet autoantibodies (GAD) confirm autoimmune type 1.
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium, high PTH, low phosphate.
  • Secondary hyperparathyroidism (CKD, low vitamin D): low/normal calcium, high PTH.
exam_pearl: Hypercalcemia can also cause polyuria, but the diagnosis question here is anchored by HbA1c plus low C-peptide, not by the calcium.
compiler_note: Compiler note: HbA1c 8.5% confirms DM; very low C-peptide = little or no endogenous insulin = Type 1 DM (normal/high C-peptide = T2DM or MODY). Can occur in adults (LADA). High calcium and PTH suggest primary hyperparathyroidism, a separate condition not changing the diabetes diagnosis.

stem: 50-year-old man presents for a routine follow-up. He has no history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or hypertension. On high dose of atorvastatins. His physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory investigations reveal: cholesterol: within normal range Triglycerides: significantly elevated (2.8) normal (2.2). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Cholesterol is normal on a high-dose statin, and the only abnormality is a mildly raised triglyceride (2.8 mmol/L). The LDL goal is already met, so the remaining step among the options is a triglyceride-lowering agent: omega-3 fatty acids, alongside lifestyle measures (weight, alcohol, refined carbohydrates).
why_wrong_block:
A. He is already on high-dose atorvastatin with normal cholesterol; more statin adds little triglyceride lowering. It would be right if LDL were above target on a lower dose.
C. Niacin lowers triglycerides but added to a statin gave no cardiovascular benefit in trials and causes flushing, hyperglycemia and hepatotoxicity, so it is no longer recommended.
D. Evolocumab (PCSK9 inhibitor) lowers LDL for high-risk patients above LDL target on maximal statin; LDL is fine here and it barely affects triglycerides.
key_concept:
Residual high triglycerides on a statin: fix lifestyle and secondary causes, then add a TG agent.
  • Check secondary causes: obesity, alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes, hypothyroidism, drugs.
  • Omega-3 (icosapent ethyl): outcome benefit shown in ASCVD or diabetes with residual high TG on statin.
  • Fibrates: main choice when TG is very high (pancreatitis risk).
  • LDL above target on max statin: add ezetimibe, then PCSK9 inhibitor.
  • Niacin: no longer recommended.
exam_pearl: Very high triglycerides (pancreatitis range) point to a fibrate; a mild rise with LDL at goal on a statin points to lifestyle plus omega-3.

stem: A patient recently treated for tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is being evaluated for resumption of chemotherapy. Laboratory values show: Uric acid: 460 umol/L; Creatinine: 135 umol/L; Blood pH: 7.2. Which of the following criteria best indicate readiness to resume chemotherapy?
why_right: The lead-in asks which criteria set shows readiness to resume chemotherapy, and this recall's key is B because the patient's own values all satisfy it: uric acid 460 (< 475), creatinine 135 (< 141) and pH 7.2 (≥ 7). A uric acid below about 475 umol/L sits under the laboratory TLS threshold (476 umol/L, equal to 8 mg/dL), so the hyperuricemia has resolved. Treat this as a matching exercise: pick the set the given numbers fit and that is physiologically possible.
why_wrong_block:
A. A uric acid cut-off of 375 is stricter than the TLS threshold; this patient (460) would wrongly be held back despite recovery.
C. A blood pH of 8 or more is not compatible with life, so this criterion can never be a readiness target.
key_concept:
TLS: know the lab pattern and the uric acid threshold.
  • Pattern: high potassium, high phosphate, high uric acid, low calcium.
  • Uric acid TLS threshold: 476 umol/L (8 mg/dL).
  • Clinical TLS adds AKI, arrhythmia or seizures.
  • Prevention: IV hydration plus allopurinol; rasburicase for high risk or established hyperuricemia.
  • Resume chemotherapy once electrolytes, uric acid and renal function have recovered.
exam_pearl: When options differ only in thresholds, test the patient's own numbers against each set and discard any physiologically impossible value.

stem: A 60-year-old patient is on lisinopril, thiazide diuretic, and atorvastatin. He presents with muscle weakness and generalized muscle aches. Which medication is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
highlight_terms_source: muscle weakness and generalized muscle aches
why_right: Muscle weakness with generalized muscle aches in a patient on atorvastatin is statin-associated muscle symptoms (myalgia to myopathy, rarely rhabdomyolysis). It is the classic statin adverse effect; check CK (and renal function) and hold or change the statin if CK is raised or symptoms are intolerable.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lisinopril causes dry cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia and a creatinine rise, not myalgia.
B. Thiazides can cause weakness through hypokalemia or hyponatremia; this would be the answer if low potassium or cramps with electrolyte changes were reported, but diffuse muscle aches point to the statin.
key_concept:
Statin muscle symptoms: check CK.
  • Myalgia: aches with normal CK.
  • Myopathy/myositis: weakness with raised CK.
  • Rhabdomyolysis: very high CK, dark urine, AKI.
  • Risk rises with high dose and interacting drugs (fibrates, macrolides, azoles).
  • Thiazide effects: low K, low Na, high Ca, high uric acid, high glucose.
exam_pearl: Aches plus weakness on a statin = statin myopathy; weakness with low potassium on a thiazide = the diuretic.

stem: 70 years old male with case of bicuspid aortic stenosis and LVH, normal EF, no LV dilation, with no symptoms; what is the management?
why_right: Valve intervention in aortic stenosis is driven by symptoms (angina, syncope, dyspnea) or LV dysfunction, not by the lesion alone. This patient has no symptoms, normal EF and no LV dilation; LVH is the expected compensatory response to pressure overload, not an indication for surgery. He is therefore managed with follow-up (clinical review and serial echocardiography) and prompt intervention once symptoms appear.
why_wrong_block:
A. TAVR is for symptomatic severe AS (or EF reduced), particularly in older or higher surgical risk patients; with no symptoms and normal EF it is not indicated, and a bicuspid valve is also less favourable anatomy for TAVR.
B. Surgical valve replacement would be the answer if he became symptomatic or the EF fell; even then, at 70 a bioprosthetic valve is usually favoured over a mechanical valve, which commits him to lifelong warfarin.
key_concept:
Aortic stenosis rule: asymptomatic with normal EF = follow-up; symptoms or falling EF = replace.
  • AS triad: angina, exertional syncope, dyspnea/heart failure
  • Asymptomatic severe AS with normal EF: serial echo follow-up
  • Symptoms or EF reduced: aortic valve replacement
  • Surgical AVR vs TAVR: by age and surgical risk
  • Mechanical valve: younger patients; bioprosthetic: older patients
  • Avoid vasodilators/diuretics that drop preload in AS
exam_pearl: Add a single symptom (syncope, angina, dyspnea) or a falling EF to the same stem and the answer flips to valve replacement.

stem: Pt post some cholangitis intervention; few hours later he develops chills and rigor. Only fever mentioned: RR 18, HR 92, Bp 115/88, Temp 38, WBC low. Diagnosis:
why_right: This recall's key is SIRS because the vitals meet two SIRS criteria: HR 92 (above 90) and a low WBC (below 4,000). Temperature 38 is not above 38 and RR 18 is not above 20, so they do not count. The source reads chills and rigors after biliary instrumentation as an inflammatory response without confirmed infection, and the BP of 115/88 excludes shock.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sepsis is SIRS plus a confirmed or presumed infection; the source did not treat infection as established here, but it would be the answer if a source (positive cultures, infected stent, cholangitis) were clearly stated.
C. Bacteremia is the answer when rigors follow biliary instrumentation but no SIRS criterion is met (HR below 90, normal WBC); here HR and WBC fulfil two criteria.
D. Septic shock needs sepsis with hypotension refractory to fluids requiring vasopressors (MAP below 65); this patient is normotensive at 115/88.
key_concept:
SIRS-era continuum: count criteria, then add infection, organ failure, shock.
  • Temp >38 or <36; HR >90; RR >20 or PaCO2 <32; WBC >12,000 or <4,000 or >10% bands
  • SIRS: 2 or more criteria
  • Sepsis: SIRS plus confirmed or presumed infection
  • Severe sepsis: sepsis plus organ dysfunction
  • Septic shock: refractory hypotension needing vasopressors
  • Rigors after instrumentation with 0 criteria: bacteremia
exam_pearl: Exactly 38 does not count; the threshold is above 38. Recount every vital: one extra criterion or an explicit infection source flips the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot: 'Right is: B) Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS)'.

stem: An 18-year man is complaining of red Urine for 5 days. He has no abdominal pain and no dysuria, urgency or frequency. His history is significant for tonsillitis 3 weeks ago. Physical examination is normal except for elevated blood pressure. Blood pressure 160/100 mmHg, Heart rate 76/min. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Painless red urine with hypertension 160/100 appearing 3 weeks after tonsillitis is a nephritic picture after a latent period, which is classic post-streptococcal (post-infectious) glomerulonephritis. The absence of pain and lower urinary symptoms points away from stones and infection, and the 1 to 3 week gap is the key timing clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. Kidney stone: causes colicky flank or abdominal pain radiating to the groin; this patient has no pain and no link to a throat infection.
B. Hypernephroma (renal cell carcinoma): painless hematuria in an older adult, often with a flank mass or pain; unlikely in an 18-year-old 3 weeks after tonsillitis.
C. IgA nephropathy: hematuria starts within a few days of the infection (synpharyngitic); here the gap is 3 weeks, which fits PSGN.
key_concept:
Hematuria after a throat infection: the latent period decides the diagnosis.
  • Within 1 to 3 days (during the infection) = IgA nephropathy
  • 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis (longer after impetigo) = PSGN
  • PSGN = nephritic: hematuria, hypertension, edema, low C3
  • IgA nephropathy: normal C3, recurrent episodes
exam_pearl: Same stem but hematuria 1 to 2 days after the sore throat flips the answer to IgA nephropathy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Confirmed by Master the Board (per screenshot).

stem: An elderly patient presents with fever, dysuria, and confusion. He has a history of hypertension. Sodium (Na+): 132 mmol/L; Calcium (Ca2+): 1.6 mmol/L; Urinalysis: leukocytes present; Blood pressure: elevated. Which of the following treatments will reverse the CNS symptoms?
why_right: An elderly patient with fever, dysuria and leukocytes in the urine has a urinary tract infection, and the new confusion is delirium driven by that infection. Delirium resolves when its cause is treated, so appropriate antibiotics are what reverse the CNS symptoms. A sodium of 132 is only mildly low and would not by itself explain acute confusion.
why_wrong_block:
A. Correct hyponatremia: Na 132 is mild; confusion from hyponatremia usually occurs with much lower or rapidly falling levels. It would be right with severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma).
B. IV calcium gluconate: used for symptomatic or severe hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures, prolonged QT) or hyperkalemia; the clinical picture here is infection, not tetany.
C. IV fluids: supportive if dehydrated or hypotensive, but fluids do not remove the cause of the delirium; BP here is elevated, not low.
key_concept:
Acute confusion in an elderly patient = delirium until proven otherwise; treat the precipitant.
  • Commonest triggers: infection (UTI, pneumonia), drugs, electrolytes, retention, constipation
  • Fever + dysuria + pyuria = UTI as the driver
  • Mild hyponatremia (low 130s) rarely causes confusion
  • Treating the cause reverses delirium
exam_pearl: In an elderly patient with fever and urinary findings, look past a minor lab abnormality: the infection is the cause of the confusion.

stem: A 62-Year-Old Woman With Atrial Fibrillation On Warfarin Develops A Subdural Hematoma. Her INR = 3.9, And She Has Already Received Vitamin K. The Hematoma Requires Urgent Surgical Evacuation. What Is The Most Appropriate Next Step In Management?
why_right: A subdural hematoma on warfarin is life-threatening bleeding that needs urgent surgical evacuation, so the INR (3.9) must be reversed immediately whatever its value. Vitamin K has already been given but takes hours to work, so a rapid factor replacement is still needed. 4-factor PCC replaces factors II, VII, IX and X in a small volume within minutes and is preferred over FFP for urgent warfarin reversal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Restarting warfarin with an active intracranial bleed and pending surgery would worsen bleeding; anticoagulation is resumed only later, after hemostasis, on specialist judgement.
B. FFP also replaces clotting factors but needs a large volume, thawing and cross-matching, so it is slower and risks fluid overload; it is the fallback when PCC is not available.
C. Recombinant activated factor VII is not part of the standard warfarin reversal algorithm and carries thrombotic risk; it is not recommended for this indication.
key_concept:
Warfarin and high INR: is there bleeding?
  • Major/life-threatening bleed: stop warfarin, IV vitamin K plus PCC (or FFP if PCC unavailable)
  • No bleed, INR >10: hold warfarin, oral vitamin K, close follow-up
  • No bleed, INR 4.5 to 10: hold warfarin, recheck INR; vitamin K not routinely needed
  • PCC: fast, small volume, preferred
  • Vitamin K: slow but sustained; always add it
exam_pearl: If the options offer 'FFP and vitamin K' but no PCC, that combination is the keyed answer; when PCC is listed and vitamin K is already given, choose PCC.

Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0321).
Compiler note: Duplicate of 321.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has had mild intermittent asthma for years. She uses a short-acting bronchodilator, as needed. Over the past 2 months, she has noticed that she is using her inhaler at least 3 times a week, and on occasions has had to wake up in the middle of the night to use her inhaler. Which of the following treatments should be added?
highlight_terms_source: using her inhaler at least 3 times a week
wake up in the middle of the night
why_right: She is on step 1 (SABA as needed) and is now poorly controlled: reliever use at least 3 times a week and night waking for 2 months. Uncontrolled asthma on SABA alone means stepping up to a daily controller, and the preferred step 2 controller is a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid.
why_wrong_block:
A. Leukotriene receptor antagonist: an alternative or add-on controller used later in the ladder (or if ICS cannot be used); not the preferred first controller.
B. Long-acting beta-agonist: added on top of ICS at step 3; LABA without ICS increases asthma deaths and must never be used alone.
D. Cromolyn: a mast cell stabilizer with weak efficacy; not a preferred controller in current guidelines.
key_concept:
Asthma step-up ladder:
  • Step 1: SABA as needed
  • Step 2: add low-dose ICS (first controller)
  • Step 3: low-dose ICS + LABA
  • Step 4: medium/high-dose ICS + LABA, consider LTRA
  • Night waking or frequent reliever use = uncontrolled, step up
  • Check inhaler technique and adherence before stepping up
exam_pearl: LABA alone is always wrong in asthma: it is only ever added to an ICS.

stem: Old patient with type 1 DM was sitting in the waiting area of outpatient clinic; after a while patient developed symptoms of hypoglycemia; they checked blood sugar, it was low. Next step?
why_right: The patient is sitting in the waiting area and developed symptoms, so he is conscious and able to swallow. A conscious hypoglycemic patient is treated with fast-acting oral carbohydrate such as juice, then glucose is rechecked after about 15 minutes and repeated if still low. IV access is not needed when the oral route is safe.
why_wrong_block:
B. 0.9% normal saline: contains no glucose, so it does nothing for hypoglycemia; it is a fluid for volume depletion, not low sugar.
C. 5% dextrose IV: slower and unnecessary when he can swallow, and 5% is too dilute for rapid correction; IV dextrose (10% or higher) is for patients who are unconscious or cannot swallow and have IV access.
key_concept:
Hypoglycemia treatment depends on consciousness and ability to swallow.
  • Conscious, can swallow: 15 g fast carbohydrate (juice, glucose tablets), recheck in 15 min, repeat
  • Unconscious or cannot swallow, no IV: IM/SC glucagon
  • Unconscious with IV access: IV concentrated dextrose
  • Follow with a longer-acting carbohydrate once recovered
exam_pearl: Drowsy is not unconscious: if he can swallow, oral glucose comes first.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot note: if the patient is conscious and able to swallow, providing a source of rapidly absorbed (glucose).

stem: A patient with sickle cell disease presents with acute chest syndrome and bilateral lung infiltrates on chest X-ray. What is the most appropriate treatment?
why_right: Acute chest syndrome with bilateral lung infiltrates indicates severe disease, and severe acute chest syndrome is an indication for exchange transfusion. Exchange transfusion rapidly lowers the HbS percentage without raising viscosity, which improves oxygenation and halts further sickling in the lungs. It is given alongside oxygen, fluids, analgesia and antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Allopurinol: lowers uric acid (gout, tumor lysis); it has no role in treating acute chest syndrome.
B. Hydroxyurea: raises HbF and is the long-term drug to PREVENT recurrent ACS and pain crises; it does not treat an acute severe episode.
D. Methotrexate: an antimetabolite and immunosuppressant (RA, malignancy, ectopic pregnancy); no role in sickle cell disease.
key_concept:
Acute chest syndrome: treat now vs prevent later.
  • All cases: oxygen, hydration, analgesia, broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Mild ACS: simple transfusion
  • Severe ACS (multilobar or bilateral, worsening hypoxia): exchange transfusion
  • Other exchange indications: stroke, priapism, retinal infarction
  • Prevention of recurrence: hydroxyurea
exam_pearl: 'Most appropriate treatment' of an acute severe episode = exchange transfusion; 'reduce future episodes' = hydroxyurea.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 3× in this file (also AS-0317, AS-0349).

stem: A 40-year-old male, 5-pack-year smoker presents to the Emergency Room with a sudden onset of retrosternal chest pain radiating to the neck. His blood pressure is 150/92. ECG: ST-segment depression in II, III, and aVF. Which of the following is the most considerable risk factor?
why_right: This recall's key is hypertension: the patient has a raised BP (150/92) at presentation with an acute coronary syndrome (inferior ST depression), and hypertension is one of the most important and prevalent risk factors for coronary disease. His smoking history is modest (5 pack-years), and at 40 he is below the usual age threshold at which male age counts as a risk factor.
why_wrong_block:
A. Smoking: a strong modifiable risk factor, but the exposure here is light (5 pack-years); it would be the intended answer if the stem stressed heavy or long-standing smoking.
B. Male gender: a non-modifiable risk factor, but on its own it carries less weight than an established condition like hypertension.
C. Patient's age: age counts as a coronary risk factor from about 45 in men; at 40 he does not meet that threshold.
key_concept:
Coronary artery disease risk factors:
  • Modifiable: hypertension, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, obesity, inactivity
  • Non-modifiable: age (men ≥45, women ≥55), male sex, family history of premature CAD
  • Inferior leads = II, III, aVF
  • When choosing the 'most important' factor, look for the one the stem quantifies as abnormal
exam_pearl: If the stem gave heavy pack-years or diabetes, that would become the dominant risk factor.

stem: Patient had chemotherapy, after 1 day (written like this) developed fever, labs showed low WBC and low neutrophils. What to do?
why_right: Fever after chemotherapy with low WBC and neutrophils is febrile neutropenia, a medical emergency. After cultures are taken, empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics must start immediately because infection can progress to septic shock within hours.
why_wrong_block:
B. Close observation: delays treatment in a patient with no neutrophil defence; observation is never acceptable in febrile neutropenia.
C. Antibiotic and antiviral: antivirals are added only for a specific indication (suspected herpes or influenza), not as routine initial therapy.
D. Oral antibiotic and antifungal: oral therapy is reserved for selected low-risk outpatients, and antifungals are added only if fever persists despite several days of antibiotics.
key_concept:
Febrile neutropenia: culture, then IV antibiotics without delay.
  • Any chemo patient with fever = treat as neutropenic until proven otherwise
  • Blood (and other) cultures, then empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotic (anti-pseudomonal)
  • Add vancomycin only for specific indications (line infection, MRSA, instability)
  • Persistent fever after several days: add antifungal
  • Antivirals only for a specific indication
exam_pearl: Do not wait for culture results or a focus: start IV antibiotics as soon as cultures are drawn.

stem: A 30 yo patient with persistent HTN despite being on 2 antihypertensive medications. Laboratory investigations show hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. What is the most appropriate next step to identify the underlying cause of hypertension?
highlight_terms_source: persistent HTN despite being on 2 antihypertensive
why_right: A 30-year-old with resistant hypertension plus hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis fits primary hyperaldosteronism: excess aldosterone retains sodium and wastes potassium and hydrogen ions. The screening test is the plasma aldosterone:renin ratio, which is high because aldosterone is raised while renin is suppressed.
why_wrong_block:
A. 24-hour urine cortisol: screens for Cushing syndrome, which would show cushingoid features (central obesity, striae, proximal weakness); none are described.
C. Plasma metanephrines: screen for pheochromocytoma, which presents with paroxysmal headache, sweating and palpitations, not hypokalemic alkalosis.
D. Renal artery Doppler: for suspected renal artery stenosis (elderly vasculopath, asymmetric kidneys, bruit, creatinine rise on ACE inhibitor); RAS can also cause hypokalemia, but renin would be high, and the ratio test comes first in this picture.
key_concept:
Secondary hypertension clue to first test:
  • HTN + hypokalemia ± metabolic alkalosis: aldosterone:renin ratio (Conn)
  • Paroxysmal headache, sweating, palpitations: plasma or urine metanephrines
  • Cushingoid features: 24-h urine cortisol or dexamethasone suppression test
  • Elderly atherosclerosis, asymmetric kidneys: renal artery imaging
  • Young woman: fibromuscular dysplasia
exam_pearl: Hypokalemic alkalosis with high renin points to renal artery stenosis; with suppressed renin it is primary hyperaldosteronism.

stem: A 64-year-old man presented to Emergency Room with symptoms of dyspnoea, SOB, and palpitation. He is a known case of diabetic mellitus, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. He is smoker with history of stroke. On examination, found to have irregular pulse. Cardiac and chest examination showed high JVP, S3 and bi-basal crackles. Atrial fibrillation on ECG. Blood pressure 150/90 mmH Heart rate 144 /min Oxygen saturation 89 % What is the CHADS2 score of this patient?
highlight_terms_source: high JVP, S3 and bi-basal crackles
why_right: CHADS2 adds: CHF 1 (high JVP, S3, bi-basal crackles), hypertension 1, age ≥75 0 (he is 64), diabetes 1, and prior stroke 2. The total is 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 2 = 5. Smoking and hyperlipidemia are not scored.
why_wrong_block:
A. 2: counts only the stroke points and misses heart failure, hypertension and diabetes.
B. 3: undercounts, usually by scoring stroke as 1 and missing the heart failure signs, or by leaving out two items.
C. 4: misses one item, most often the heart failure (raised JVP, S3, crackles), or scores stroke as 1 instead of 2.
key_concept:
CHADS2 (max 6):
  • C: congestive heart failure = 1
  • H: hypertension = 1
  • A: age ≥75 = 1
  • D: diabetes = 1
  • S2: prior stroke or TIA = 2
  • Not scored: smoking, hyperlipidemia
exam_pearl: Stroke/TIA is worth 2 points, and clinical heart failure signs in the stem count as the C.
compiler_note: Compiler note: ✅MG. CHF: Yes (S3, crackles, high JVP) = 1 point; Hypertension: Yes = 1 point; Age ≥75: No (64 y) = 0 points; Diabetes mellitus: Yes = 1 point; Stroke history: Yes = 2 points. Total 5.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presented to the clinic with a 3-month history of fatigue, lethargy and weight gain. Physical examination is unremarkable (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
why_right: "Fatigue, lethargy and weight gain" over 3 months with a normal exam raises suspicion of hypothyroidism. TSH is the single best first test for thyroid dysfunction because it is the most sensitive marker of primary thyroid disease; further tests depend on its result.
why_wrong_block:
B. TPO antibodies identify the cause (Hashimoto thyroiditis) once dysfunction is confirmed, or guide management of subclinical hypothyroidism; they are not the first test.
C. T3 is not used to assess hypothyroidism and is measured, if at all, after TSH (mainly in suspected T3 toxicosis).
D. Free T4 is checked after an abnormal TSH (or together with it if pituitary disease is suspected); alone it is not the initial screen.
key_concept:
Thyroid work up ladder: TSH first.
  • Step 1: TSH
  • Step 2: free T4 (± T3) if TSH abnormal
  • Step 3: TPO antibodies for the cause (Hashimoto)
  • High TSH + low fT4 = overt primary hypothyroidism
  • High TSH + normal fT4 = subclinical hypothyroidism
exam_pearl: TPO is tempting because Hashimoto is common in young women, but you confirm dysfunction (TSH) before looking for its cause.

stem: Elderly patient k/c of DM and HTN and post MI he is on multiple med (important is MAX DOSE OF ATORVASTATIN) present to clinic for regular follow up His LDL was 4.2 can't remember HDL sorry What would you add?
why_right: This is a very high-risk patient (post-MI, diabetes, hypertension) whose LDL is 4.2 despite the maximum dose of atorvastatin. When the LDL target is not reached on a maximally tolerated statin, the next step is to add ezetimibe, which lowers LDL further by blocking intestinal cholesterol absorption.
why_wrong_block: A. No change: leaving an LDL of 4.2 in a post-MI patient is far above secondary prevention targets; no change would only be right if LDL were already at target.
key_concept:
Lipid lowering in established ASCVD:
  • Start high-intensity statin regardless of baseline LDL
  • Not at target on maximal tolerated statin: add ezetimibe
  • Still not at target: consider a PCSK9 inhibitor
  • Statin intolerant: ezetimibe or other non-statin agents
  • Fibrates and niacin are not used for LDL secondary prevention
exam_pearl: If the stem says the patient is NOT on a statin, the answer is a high-intensity statin, not ezetimibe.

stem: 55 yo male hx of inferior MI (on aspirin, etc..) and max dose of atorvastatin came to f/u lipid profile results HDL 1.3 N LDL 4.? (High)
why_right: This recall's key is evolocumab (a PCSK9 inhibitor). He has clinical ASCVD (prior inferior MI) and his LDL is still high (about 4 mmol/L) despite maximum dose atorvastatin, so he is very far above the secondary prevention target. Ezetimibe adds only a modest extra LDL reduction and would not close a gap this large, whereas a PCSK9 inhibitor gives a large further fall in LDL and has proven event reduction on top of a statin.
why_wrong_block: A. Ezetimibe is the usual first add on to a maximally tolerated statin when LDL is modestly above target, or when a PCSK9 inhibitor is unavailable; with LDL this far above goal it is unlikely to reach target alone, which is why this recall keys the more potent agent.
key_concept:
Secondary prevention lipid ladder: high intensity statin first, then add on therapy if LDL stays above target.
  • Clinical ASCVD (MI, ACS, stroke, PAD) = high intensity statin regardless of baseline LDL
  • Still above target on max statin, small gap: add ezetimibe
  • Still above target on statin + ezetimibe, or very large gap: add PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab, alirocumab)
  • Niacin and fibrates: no proven outcome benefit on top of statins
exam_pearl: LDL only slightly above target on max statin points to ezetimibe; LDL still markedly high on max statin in very high risk ASCVD points to a PCSK9 inhibitor.

stem: 52 years come from holiday he was abroad, diagnosed with pneumonia and failed to respond to course of amoxicillin. On admission he is complaining of cough, myalgia and abdominal pain, X-ray shows bilateral basal opacities. His GCS dropped to 11. Temp 38.5 Oxygen 91 Na 118 Creatinine 180 Which of the following is the cause:
highlight_terms_source: come from holiday he was abroad
failed to respond to course of amoxicillin
why_right: Legionnaires' disease fits every clue: recent travel abroad (hotel water systems, air conditioning), pneumonia that failed amoxicillin (an intracellular organism not covered by beta lactams), extrapulmonary features (myalgia, abdominal pain, confusion with GCS 11), hyponatremia (Na 118) and raised creatinine. Bilateral infiltrates with high fever complete an atypical, severe pneumonia picture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sarcoidosis is a chronic granulomatous disease with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, dry cough and progressive dyspnea; it does not cause an acute febrile pneumonia with confusion and hyponatremia after travel.
C. Pulmonary embolism presents with sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain and hypoxia; it does not produce a febrile illness with GI symptoms, hyponatremia and failed antibiotic therapy.
D. ANCA associated vasculitis can give pulmonary infiltrates with renal failure (pulmonary renal syndrome), but expect hemoptysis, sinus disease or hematuria with active sediment, not a travel related febrile pneumonia with marked hyponatremia and GI upset.
key_concept:
Legionella = atypical pneumonia with systemic and extrapulmonary features.
  • Source: contaminated water (hotels, cruise ships, air conditioning), travel history
  • Clues: high fever, confusion, diarrhea or abdominal pain, myalgia
  • Labs: hyponatremia, deranged LFTs, raised creatinine
  • Fails beta lactams (amoxicillin)
  • Diagnosis: urinary antigen test
  • Treatment: macrolide or respiratory fluoroquinolone
exam_pearl: Pneumonia + hyponatremia + GI symptoms + confusion after travel, not responding to amoxicillin = Legionella until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient was bitten by a bat, what is the most likely infection?
why_right: Bats are a classic reservoir of rabies, and a bat bite (even a minor or unnoticed one) is a high risk rabies exposure. The infection the question is testing is therefore rabies, which is almost always fatal once symptoms start, so post exposure prophylaxis must begin promptly.
why_wrong_block: B. Tetanus comes from Clostridium tetani spores in soil contaminating any dirty or deep wound; tetanus status should be checked for any bite, but it is not the infection specifically linked to a bat.
key_concept:
Animal bite: think of the specific organism by animal.
  • Bat, fox, raccoon, stray dog: rabies, give post exposure prophylaxis
  • Rabies PEP: thorough wound washing + rabies vaccine series + rabies immunoglobulin (if not previously vaccinated)
  • Cat bite: Pasteurella multocida (treat with amoxicillin clavulanate)
  • Human bite: Eikenella, mixed oral flora
  • Any wound: check tetanus immunization status
exam_pearl: Any bat contact with a possible bite counts as a rabies exposure; do not wait for symptoms, start PEP.

stem: A 50-year-old man known to have chronic viral hepatitis presented with ascites and was found to have a high serum ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) of more than 1.1. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
highlight_terms_source: high serum ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) of more than 1.1
why_right: A SAAG of more than 1.1 g/dL means the ascites is due to portal hypertension. In a man with chronic viral hepatitis, the cause of portal hypertension is liver cirrhosis. All the other options produce low-SAAG ascites.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pancreatic ascites is low SAAG (exudative, high amylase); right with a history of pancreatitis or pseudocyst.
B. Tuberculous peritonitis is low SAAG with lymphocytic, high-protein fluid; right with fever, weight loss and low SAAG.
D. Nephrotic syndrome causes low SAAG ascites from hypoalbuminemia, not portal hypertension; right with heavy proteinuria and edema.
key_concept:
SAAG algorithm
  • SAAG ≥1.1 = portal hypertension
  • ≥1.1 + ascitic protein <2.5 = cirrhosis, late Budd-Chiari, massive liver metastases
  • ≥1.1 + protein ≥2.5 = heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, early Budd-Chiari
  • SAAG <1.1 = TB, peritoneal carcinomatosis, pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome, biliary leak
exam_pearl: High SAAG = portal hypertension; then ascitic protein separates liver (low) from heart (high).

stem: A 32-Year-Old Man Came To The Clinic For A Follow-Up Visit. He Is Diagnosed Of Ileocolonic Crohn’s Disease Started On Steroids And Pentasa For 3 Months. He Noticed Perineal Pain And Discharges For 3 Weeks Duration. His Abdominal Symptoms Are Well Controlled With No Abdominal Pain Or Diarrhea. Examination Was Normal Apart From 2 Perianal Fistula Were Seen. RBC 4 (4.7–6.1 × 10¹²/L) Hb 11 (130–170 g/L) Platelets Count 421 (150–400 × 10⁹/L) WBC 7 (4.5–10.5 × 10⁹/L) ESR 36 (2–10 mm/h) MRI Pelvis: Confirmed The Presence Of Perianal Fistulae. Which Of The Following Is The Best Next Step In Management?
why_right: Luminal Crohn's is controlled, but he now has two perianal fistulae confirmed on MRI pelvis. Fistulizing Crohn's disease is an indication for anti-TNF biologic therapy, and infliximab is the agent with the strongest evidence for fistula closure and maintenance. The other options do not heal fistulae on their own.
why_wrong_block:
A. Methotrexate: an immunomodulator for steroid dependent luminal Crohn's (or alongside a biologic); it is not the treatment of choice for perianal fistulae.
B. Azathioprine: slow acting maintenance immunomodulator; alone it is insufficient for fistulizing disease and is mainly used in combination with infliximab.
C. Budesonide: an ileal release steroid for inducing remission in mild to moderate ileocecal luminal disease; steroids do not heal fistulae and are not for maintenance.
key_concept:
Crohn's ladder: steroids induce, immunomodulators maintain, biologics for refractory or FISTULIZING disease.
  • Induction: budesonide (ileal) or IV methylprednisolone (severe)
  • Maintenance: azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate
  • Fistulizing or refractory: infliximab or adalimumab (often with azathioprine)
  • Perianal sepsis: MRI pelvis to map; drain any abscess (seton) before biologics
  • Screen for TB and hepatitis B before anti-TNF
exam_pearl: Perianal fistula in Crohn's = anti-TNF (infliximab); if the stem adds fever and fluctuance, the next step is imaging and drainage first.

stem: A patient presents with the following neurological findings Extraocular movement (EOM) weakness, Vertical nystagmus, Reactive miosis, Dysarthria and Ataxia Where is the most likely lesion?
why_right: All the findings are brainstem and cerebellar: extraocular movement weakness, vertical nystagmus, miosis (pontine sympathetic pathway), dysarthria and ataxia. These structures are supplied by the vertebrobasilar system, and in a diabetic, hypertensive patient a basilar artery lesion is the unifying site.
why_wrong_block:
B. Anterior cerebral artery stroke gives contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss, urinary incontinence and behavioural change, not cranial nerve or cerebellar signs.
C. Middle cerebral artery stroke gives contralateral face and arm weakness, aphasia (dominant side) or neglect (non dominant side) and hemianopia; it does not cause nystagmus, miosis or ataxia.
D. Posterior cerebral artery stroke gives contralateral homonymous hemianopia, visual agnosia and memory loss; it would be the answer if the main finding were a visual field defect rather than brainstem signs.
key_concept:
Localise by the cluster of signs.
  • ACA: contralateral leg weakness, incontinence, behaviour change
  • MCA: contralateral face and arm weakness, aphasia or neglect, hemianopia
  • PCA: contralateral homonymous hemianopia, visual agnosia, memory
  • Basilar (brainstem): cranial nerve palsies, nystagmus, pinpoint pupils, dysarthria, ataxia, may progress to coma or locked in
  • Crossed signs (ipsilateral cranial nerve, contralateral body) = brainstem
exam_pearl: Eye movement problems + nystagmus + ataxia + dysarthria = posterior circulation brainstem, i.e. basilar, not the cortical ACA/MCA/PCA territories.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall: 'Known case of DM, HTN with 6 months history of impairment of extraocular muscles, nystagmus, ataxia, dysarthria. What is the affected area?' Answer: A (Basilar artery).

stem: 26 y.o man with history of fatigue for one month. He was diagnosed with AML 5Ma, and one day before starting chemotherapy, he had high grade fever. Labs show WBC 3 (low), neutrophils 0.2% (low), Hgb 6 (low), platelet 100 (low) What is the best medication to start with?
why_right: This is febrile neutropenia: AML with high grade fever and a very low neutrophil count (WBC 3 with neutrophils almost absent). It is a medical emergency needing empiric IV broad spectrum antibiotics with antipseudomonal cover. An extended spectrum (antipseudomonal) penicillin such as piperacillin tazobactam is a standard first line monotherapy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fluoroquinolones are used as prophylaxis during expected neutropenia or, with amoxicillin clavulanate, as oral therapy for low risk outpatients; a newly diagnosed AML patient with profound neutropenia is high risk and needs IV therapy.
B. G-CSF may shorten neutropenia but does not treat the infection and is not routinely used for established febrile neutropenia, especially in myeloid leukemia; antibiotics come first.
D. Ceftriaxone and cefotaxime, the usual third generation cephalosporins, lack Pseudomonas cover; ceftazidime does cover it but has weak gram positive activity and is no longer preferred. First line is an antipseudomonal beta lactam such as piperacillin tazobactam, cefepime or a carbapenem.
key_concept:
Febrile neutropenia = fever + neutrophils below 0.5 (or expected to fall): emergency.
  • Take cultures (blood, urine, sputum) but do not delay antibiotics
  • Start empiric IV antipseudomonal beta lactam monotherapy: piperacillin tazobactam, cefepime or a carbapenem
  • Add vancomycin only for specific indications (line infection, MRSA, instability)
  • Add antifungal only if fever persists despite several days of antibiotics
  • Oral fluoroquinolone + amoxicillin clavulanate only for low risk patients
exam_pearl: Ceftriaxone is not antipseudomonal; in febrile neutropenia choose the antipseudomonal penicillin (piperacillin tazobactam).

stem: 50 yo male newly diagnosed with bulky diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), came to ER c/o N&V, decreased urine output for 24 h after first cycle of chemotherapy (R CHOP) K 6 PO4 3 Ca 1.2 UA 570 What is the drug that help in prevent such presentation?
highlight_terms_source: bulky diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
after first cycle of chemotherapy (R CHOP)
why_right: Nausea, vomiting and oliguria after the first R-CHOP cycle with high K, high phosphate, low calcium and high uric acid is tumor lysis syndrome, and bulky DLBCL is a high risk setting. Prevention is aggressive IV hydration plus a uric acid lowering drug; among the listed options allopurinol (a xanthine oxidase inhibitor) is the one that prevents uric acid formation and uric acid nephropathy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Thiazides lower urinary calcium and are used for hypercalciuric stones; they do not prevent TLS and actually raise serum uric acid.
C. Prednisone is part of R-CHOP itself and is lympholytic, so it can contribute to tumor lysis rather than prevent it.
D. Furosemide is not a preventive drug for TLS; it may be used only to manage fluid overload once the patient is well hydrated, and hydration is the cornerstone.
key_concept:
TLS prevention depends on risk.
  • Pattern: high K, high phosphate, high uric acid, low calcium, AKI
  • All at risk: aggressive IV hydration
  • Low to intermediate risk: allopurinol (blocks xanthine oxidase, prevents new uric acid)
  • High risk or uric acid already high: rasburicase (converts existing uric acid to allantoin)
  • Rasburicase contraindicated in G6PD deficiency
exam_pearl: If rasburicase is among the options for a bulky, high risk tumor with raised uric acid, it beats allopurinol; when it is absent, allopurinol is the prevention drug.

What can prevent this presentation?' A. Thiazide B. Allopurinol C. Furosemide D. Don't remember; Answer: B. First 'Q:' version (used here) highlights Allopurinol. stem: COPD patient came with SOB for few months, NYHA2, liver enzymes slightly elevated OE, JVD, Wheezing, LLE, Ascites, loud S2, Prominent a wave. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: A COPD patient with JVD, leg edema, ascites and mildly raised liver enzymes (congestive hepatopathy) has systemic venous congestion, i.e. right heart failure. The loud S2 (loud P2) indicates pulmonary hypertension, and the prominent a wave reflects a stiff, hypertrophied right ventricle; together this is cor pulmonale.
why_wrong_block:
A. Left ventricular failure presents with orthopnea, PND and bibasal crackles from pulmonary congestion; the dominant signs here are systemic (JVD, ascites, edema) with pulmonary hypertension from lung disease.
C. Chronic liver disease can cause ascites and edema but the JVP is normal; a raised JVP with prominent a wave and loud P2 points to a cardiac cause, and the mild enzyme rise is congestive.
key_concept:
Cor pulmonale = lung disease, then pulmonary hypertension, then right heart failure.
  • Loud P2: pulmonary hypertension
  • Raised JVP, edema, ascites, tender hepatomegaly: right heart failure
  • Prominent a wave: reduced RV compliance (pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary stenosis)
  • Giant v wave: tricuspid regurgitation
  • Next step: echocardiogram
exam_pearl: Ascites with a raised JVP is cardiac (right heart failure), ascites with a normal JVP is hepatic.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents with 4 months history of diarrhea with mucus in stool and anemia. Family history: Father had colon cancer at age 60 Symptoms: Abdominal pain relieved by defecation Laboratory: ESR: Normal What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: 4 months history of diarrhea with mucus
why_right: Abdominal pain relieved by defecation with a change in bowel habit is the keyword of IBS, and mucus in the stool can occur in IBS. A normal ESR argues against an inflammatory cause, and a 23 year old with a father diagnosed at 60 is not a high risk cancer profile. The anemia is not explained by IBS and still needs checking (for example menstrual iron deficiency or celiac disease), but the source keys IBS on the defecation pattern and normal ESR.
why_wrong_block:
B. Colon cancer is unlikely at 23; a single first degree relative diagnosed at 60 changes screening age, not the likely diagnosis. It would be favoured by older age, weight loss, rectal bleeding or a strong early onset family history.
C. Ulcerative colitis presents with bloody diarrhea, nocturnal symptoms and raised inflammatory markers; a normal ESR and pain relieved by defecation favour IBS.
D. Gastroenteritis is acute and self limited, often with fever and raised inflammatory markers; it does not explain 4 months of symptoms.
key_concept:
IBS: pain related to defecation + altered bowel habit, with no alarm features and normal inflammatory markers.
  • Keyword: pain relieved by defecation
  • Mucus and bloating are allowed
  • Red flags: blood mixed with stool, nocturnal diarrhea, weight loss, older age onset, strong family history
  • Exclude: CBC, CRP, fecal calprotectin, celiac serology
  • Treat: fiber, antispasmodic, loperamide or laxative by subtype
exam_pearl: Normal ESR/CRP with pain relieved by defecation = IBS; add blood in stool or nocturnal symptoms and think UC.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall (same content, 'Answer: A') followed by a 'Q:' restatement.

stem: 62-Year-Old Woman With Atrial Fibrillation On Warfarin Develops A Subdural Hematoma. Her INR = 3.9, And She Has Already Received Vitamin K. The Hematoma Requires Urgent Surgical Evacuation. What Is The Most Appropriate Next Step In Management?
why_right: A subdural hematoma on warfarin is major bleeding, and it needs urgent evacuation, so immediate reversal is required. Vitamin K has already been given but acts over hours; the next step is immediate clotting factor replacement, and 4-factor PCC is preferred over FFP because it corrects the INR faster, in a small volume, without thawing or cross matching.
why_wrong_block:
A. Restarting warfarin during an active intracranial bleed is contraindicated; anticoagulation is only reconsidered after the bleed is controlled.
B. FFP also replaces factors and is the alternative when PCC is not available, but it corrects the INR more slowly, needs a large volume (risk of overload) and requires thawing; PCC is preferred for urgent reversal.
C. Recombinant factor VIIa is not recommended for warfarin reversal; it normalises the INR without reliably restoring hemostasis and carries thrombotic risk.
key_concept:
Warfarin reversal by bleeding status.
  • Major or life threatening bleed: IV vitamin K 10 mg + 4-factor PCC (FFP if PCC unavailable)
  • No bleeding, INR above 10: hold warfarin, oral vitamin K
  • No bleeding, INR 4 to 10: hold warfarin, consider low dose oral vitamin K
  • Vitamin K = sustained reversal over hours; PCC/FFP = immediate
  • A similar recall without PCC among the options is keyed to FFP plus vitamin K
exam_pearl: Bleeding on warfarin needs both: vitamin K for lasting effect and PCC (or FFP if PCC is not offered) for immediate effect.

stem: Ptn with non-hodgkin lymphoma and he passed away before going through chemotherapy by 1 week; he died before his chemotherapy session and he is known case of uncontrolled DM2 for 20 years and HTN. Labs: high uric acid, high potassium. What's the cause of his death?
why_right: He died before receiving chemotherapy with high uric acid and high potassium: this is spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome, which occurs in high burden, rapidly proliferating lymphomas. Released potassium causes fatal arrhythmias, and uric acid and calcium phosphate deposition cause acute kidney injury.
why_wrong_block:
A. Drug induced nephropathy needs a nephrotoxic exposure; he died before any chemotherapy was given, so no culprit drug is present.
C. Diabetic and hypertensive CKD can raise potassium, but it does not explain the lymphoma related rise in uric acid; the stem links the death to the untreated lymphoma.
D. Renal tubular acidosis (type 4 in diabetics) causes mild hyperkalemia with a non anion gap acidosis, not hyperuricemia and sudden death.
key_concept:
TLS can be spontaneous, before any chemotherapy, in bulky or fast growing tumors.
  • High risk: Burkitt and other aggressive NHL, ALL, high count leukemias, bulky disease
  • Labs: high K, high phosphate, high uric acid, low calcium, raised creatinine
  • Death: hyperkalemic arrhythmia, AKI
  • Prevention: IV hydration + allopurinol or rasburicase
exam_pearl: 'Died before chemotherapy' does not exclude TLS: aggressive lymphomas can lyse spontaneously.

stem: Known case of DM, HTN with 6 months history of impairment of extraocular muscles, nystagmus, ataxia, dysarthria. What is the affected area?
why_right: The deficits are all posterior circulation / brainstem and cerebellar signs: "impairment of extraocular muscles" (cranial nerve nuclei III, IV, VI), "nystagmus", "ataxia" and "dysarthria". The basilar artery supplies the pons, midbrain and cerebellum, and vascular risk factors ("DM, HTN") with a 6-month course fit vertebrobasilar ischemia. No anterior circulation cortical sign (aphasia, neglect, isolated limb weakness) is described.
why_wrong_block:
B. Anterior cerebral artery stroke gives contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss, urinary incontinence and behavioural change; it does not cause eye movement palsies, nystagmus or ataxia.
C. Middle cerebral artery stroke gives contralateral face and arm weakness, aphasia (dominant side) or neglect (non-dominant side) and hemianopia; brainstem signs such as ophthalmoplegia and nystagmus are absent.
D. Posterior cerebral artery stroke mainly causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia, visual agnosia and memory loss; it would be right if the stem described a visual field defect rather than brainstem and cerebellar signs.
key_concept:
Localize a stroke by its signs, not by the risk factors.
  • ACA: leg > arm weakness, incontinence, behaviour change
  • MCA: face and arm > leg, aphasia or neglect, hemianopia
  • PCA: homonymous hemianopia, visual agnosia, memory loss
  • Basilar / vertebrobasilar: diplopia or ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, vertigo, ataxia, dysarthria, crossed or bilateral deficits
  • Complete basilar occlusion can cause locked-in syndrome
exam_pearl: Cranial nerve signs plus cerebellar signs (ataxia, nystagmus, dysarthria) = brainstem = basilar territory; PCA is a branch of the basilar but presents with vision loss.

stem: A 29-year-old man diagnosed with celiac disease 2 years ago. He complains of ongoing diarrhoea, feeling tired and bloating. Poor compliance with a gluten-free diet is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate method to ascertain this?
highlight_terms_source: Poor compliance with a gluten-free diet
key_concept:
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Tissue transglutaminase antibodies.
  • Screening: tTG IgA (while eating gluten)
  • Confirmation: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes)
  • Second-line serology: anti-endomysial antibody
  • Monitoring adherence: repeat tTG IgA; should fall on a strict diet
  • Persistent symptoms with good adherence and falling serology: consider biopsy for refractory disease
exam_pearl: "Monitor compliance" in celiac disease = repeat tTG IgA; biopsy is for confirmation or refractory disease, not for checking the diet.
