stem: An elderly patient presents with exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and signs of heart failure. Echocardiography shows concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with a normal ejection fraction (60%). What is the most likely diagnosis?
OptC: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
why_right: An "elderly" patient with left-sided heart failure symptoms ("exertional dyspnea, orthopnea") and an echo showing "concentric left ventricular hypertrophy" with "normal ejection fraction (60%)" has diastolic dysfunction, i.e. HFpEF. The thick, stiff ventricle (typically from long-standing hypertension) fills poorly, so pressures rise despite normal contraction.
why_wrong_block:
A. Restrictive cardiomyopathy (e.g. amyloid) shows stiff, non-dilated ventricles with marked biatrial enlargement and often low-voltage ECG, plus right-sided signs; it would be the answer with an infiltrative clue, not a simple concentric LVH picture.
B. Constrictive pericarditis shows a thickened pericardium, pericardial knock and Kussmaul sign with right-sided congestion (often after TB or cardiac surgery); the myocardium is not hypertrophied.
D. Dilated cardiomyopathy shows a dilated ventricle with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and often an S3; here the EF is 60% and the wall is thick, not thin and dilated.
key_concept:
Heart failure is classified by ejection fraction.
  • HFrEF: EF reduced, dilated LV (systolic dysfunction)
  • HFpEF: EF ≥ 50%, concentric LVH, S4 (diastolic dysfunction)
  • Classic HFpEF patient: elderly, hypertensive, often female, diabetic or obese
  • Restrictive CMP: biatrial enlargement, low voltage, infiltrative cause
  • Constriction: Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, thick pericardium
exam_pearl: Heart failure symptoms with a normal EF and concentric LVH = HFpEF; do not jump to restrictive cardiomyopathy without biatrial enlargement or an infiltrative clue.

stem: A 25-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus on insulin therapy was found in the clinic waiting area drowsy and excessively sweating. A quick measurement of blood glucose revealed a low level. Which of the following is the most appropriate action to be taken?
why_right: This is hypoglycemia in an insulin treated patient who is "drowsy" but still conscious and able to swallow. A conscious patient is treated with fast acting oral carbohydrate (about 15 g, e.g. fruit juice), rechecking glucose after 15 minutes and repeating if still low.
why_wrong_block:
B. Normal saline contains no glucose, so it does nothing for hypoglycemia; it is used for volume depletion (e.g. DKA).
C. Glucagon is for a patient who is unconscious or cannot swallow and has no IV access; this patient is drowsy but can take oral sugar.
D. IV dextrose is for the unconscious or unable to swallow patient with IV access, and 5% dextrose is too dilute for acute rescue (10% to 50% is used).
key_concept:
Hypoglycemia: route depends on ability to swallow.
  • Conscious, can swallow: 15 g oral fast carbohydrate (juice, glucose tablets)
  • Recheck in 15 min, repeat if still low (rule of 15)
  • Then give a longer acting carbohydrate snack
  • Unconscious with IV access: IV dextrose
  • Unconscious without IV access: IM/SC glucagon
exam_pearl: "Drowsy" is not "unconscious": if the patient can swallow, oral glucose comes first.

stem: A 28-year-old man who recently joined military service and underwent excessive military training presents to the Emergency Department with lightheadedness on standing, muscle cramping, and fatigue. Physical examination reveals postural hypotension, otherwise unremarkable. A diagnosis of acute kidney injury due to hypovolemia is established. Which of the following is the most expected laboratory abnormality?
OptC: Blood urea nitrogen/creatinine ratio is elevated > 20
OptD: Presence of dysmorphic red blood cell (RBC) and RBC cast
highlight_terms_source: acute kidney injury due to hypovolemia
why_right: "Excessive military training" with "postural hypotension" and "AKI due to hypovolemia" is pre-renal AKI. Low renal perfusion triggers avid tubular reabsorption of urea (with sodium and water), while creatinine is not reabsorbed, so the BUN:creatinine ratio rises above 20. Tubules are intact, so the other indices stay in the "concentrating" range.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pre-renal AKI produces concentrated urine (osmolality > 500); a low urine osmolality < 300 reflects damaged tubules in intrinsic AKI such as ATN.
B. FeNa > 2% means the tubules are wasting sodium, as in ATN; in pre-renal AKI the kidney retains sodium, so FeNa is < 1%.
D. Dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts indicate glomerular bleeding (glomerulonephritis or vasculitis), not a perfusion problem.
key_concept:
Pre-renal vs intrinsic (ATN) AKI indices:
  • BUN:Cr: > 20 pre-renal vs < 15 ATN
  • FeNa: < 1% pre-renal vs > 2% ATN
  • Urine osmolality: > 500 pre-renal vs < 300 ATN
  • Urine sodium: low in pre-renal vs high in ATN
  • Sediment: bland in pre-renal; muddy brown casts in ATN; RBC casts in GN
exam_pearl: Pre-renal = the kidney is working hard to hold on: high BUN:Cr, low FeNa, concentrated urine.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to Emergency Department with 4-days history of fever, headache and confusion. On examination, Kernig's sign is present (see lab results and reports). Temperature 39 °C. Test / Result / Normal Values: Cells 380 (0-3 /µL); Total protein (Men) 0.8 (0.22-0.33 g/L); Glucose 3.7 (2.50-3.89 mmol/L). CSF analysis: WBC differential count: 5% neutrophil and 90% lymphocytes. CSF Culture: Pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate intravenous treatment option?
why_right: The CSF shows "90% lymphocytes" with a normal glucose (3.7 mmol/L) and only mildly raised protein, which is a viral pattern. "Confusion" over 4 days suggests encephalitic involvement, so HSV must be covered empirically with IV acyclovir while culture and PCR are pending.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceftriaxone, vancomycin and steroid is the regimen for bacterial meningitis, which shows neutrophil-predominant CSF with low glucose; that is not this picture.
B. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin is empirical bacterial coverage (e.g. neutrophilic CSF when steroids are not indicated); it does not treat HSV.
C. Ceftriaxone alone is antibacterial only (e.g. meningococcal disease) and leaves the suspected viral cause untreated.
key_concept:
Read the CSF cell type and glucose first.
  • Neutrophils + low glucose: bacterial, give ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone
  • Lymphocytes + normal glucose: viral; add acyclovir if confusion, seizures or focal signs (HSV encephalitis)
  • Lymphocytes + low glucose + high protein: TB
exam_pearl: Lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose plus confusion = cover HSV with IV acyclovir.

stem: A 22-year-old man recently returned from Umrah, presents to Emergency Department with 1-day history of fever and headache. Upon arrival to the Emergency Department, he started to have seizures on the right extremities. On examination, positive Kernig sign (see lab results and report). Temperature 39 °C. Test / Result / Normal Values: Cells 380 (0-3 /µL); Total protein (Men) 1.2 (0.22-0.33 g/L). CSF analysis: WBC differential count: 87% neutrophils and 5% lymphocytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate intravenous treatment option?
why_right: An acute ("1-day") febrile illness with seizures, positive Kernig sign and CSF showing "87% neutrophils" with high protein (1.2 g/L) is bacterial meningitis, with added risk after mass gathering ("returned from Umrah"). Empirical IV therapy in an adult is ceftriaxone (meningococcus, pneumococcus) plus vancomycin (resistant pneumococcus) plus dexamethasone given with or just before the first antibiotic dose to reduce mortality and neurological sequelae.
why_wrong_block:
B. Correct antibiotics but omits adjunctive dexamethasone; it would be the answer if steroids were not indicated (e.g. antibiotics already started well before).
C. Acyclovir targets HSV, which gives lymphocytic CSF; neutrophilic CSF points to bacteria, and this option lacks vancomycin and the steroid.
D. Acyclovir with steroid has no antibacterial cover at all, which would be dangerous in bacterial meningitis.
key_concept:
Empirical bacterial meningitis treatment in adults:
  • Ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone
  • Add ampicillin if older or immunocompromised (Listeria)
  • Viral picture (lymphocytes, normal glucose): acyclovir
  • Hajj/Umrah + petechial rash: think meningococcus, droplet precautions
exam_pearl: Neutrophilic CSF: the full answer includes the steroid; "ceftriaxone and vancomycin" alone is the incomplete trap.

stem: A 22-year-old woman was brought to the Emergency Room after ingesting 50 tablets of extra strength acetaminophen (500 mg each tablet) 3 hours ago. The patient is conscious and oriented (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptC: Close monitoring of liver function tests
highlight_terms_source: 50 tablets of extra strength acetaminophen (500 mg each tablet)
why_right: Fifty 500 mg tablets is 25 g of paracetamol, a clearly toxic ingestion, and she presents only "3 hours ago". N-acetylcysteine is the antidote (it replenishes glutathione to neutralise the toxic metabolite NAPQI), and activated charcoal still has a role this early because it reduces further absorption. A "conscious and oriented" patient can safely take charcoal, so both are given together as the next step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hemodialysis: reserved for massive paracetamol ingestion with severe metabolic acidosis or coma; this patient is alert and needs the antidote first.
C. Close monitoring of liver function tests: LFTs are normal early and liver injury peaks days later, so waiting for them only delays NAC, which works best when started early (ideally within 8 hours).
D. Intubation and mechanical ventilation: indicated only for airway compromise or coma; paracetamol does not cause early respiratory depression and she is conscious.
key_concept:
Paracetamol overdose: decontaminate early, give NAC by time and level.
  • Early presentation with a large dose: activated charcoal + NAC
  • Late presentation: NAC alone (charcoal adds little)
  • Level taken at ≥4 h and plotted on the nomogram; toxic level = NAC
  • Unknown time or >24 h: give NAC, check level and LFTs
  • Dialysis only for massive ingestion with acidosis or coma
exam_pearl: Early LFTs are normal in paracetamol toxicity, so "monitor LFTs" is the trap; never wait for liver injury before giving NAC.

stem: A 19-year-old male with known hepatitis B presents with bilateral knee pain for 2 days and has been extensively taking paracetamol. Serology: HBsAb negative, HBsAg positive, HBeAg negative, HBc IgG positive. Labs: AST >2000, ALT >1000, Bilirubin 27 (normal 5.1–17.0), INR 2.something. What is the most appropriate treatment?
OptC: Entecavir to treat acute hepatitis B
why_right: He has been taking paracetamol extensively for knee pain and now has AST over 2000, ALT over 1000, raised bilirubin and an INR above 2: acute hepatocellular injury with failing synthetic function, typical of paracetamol hepatotoxicity. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is given in any paracetamol liver injury, including staggered or repeated supratherapeutic intake where the nomogram cannot be used. His serology (HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgG positive, HBeAg negative) is background chronic hepatitis B, not the cause of this acute rise.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV corticosteroid: used for autoimmune hepatitis or severe alcoholic hepatitis; no role in paracetamol injury, and steroids can trigger a flare of hepatitis B.
C. Entecavir to treat acute hepatitis B: the serology is chronic (anti-HBc IgG, no acute markers), not acute HBV, and an antiviral does not treat drug toxicity. Right for chronic HBV with raised transaminases or active disease.
D. Plasmapheresis with penicillamine: Wilson disease therapy (copper chelation, plasmapheresis as a bridge in acute Wilsonian liver failure); right with low ceruloplasmin, Kayser Fleischer rings and Coombs negative hemolysis.
key_concept:
Paracetamol + raised transaminases = give NAC now; do not wait for a level.
  • Single acute ingestion with known time: plot level on the nomogram
  • Staggered or repeated excess use: nomogram invalid, treat if LFTs raised or level detectable
  • Markedly raised AST/ALT + rising INR = hepatotoxicity, consider liver unit referral
  • HBsAg+ / anti-HBc IgG+ = chronic HBV
  • Sudden acute hepatitis in a chronic HBV carrier without a drug cause: think HDV superinfection
exam_pearl: A known liver disease in the stem is often a distractor: the drug history (excess paracetamol) explains the acute picture.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: variant shown under 473.

stem: 70-year-old man known to have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). examination revealed evidence of cor pulmonale with a significant degree of lower limb edema. His FEV1 is 40% (see lab result). Which of the following interventions is most associated with increased survival?
why_right: This is advanced COPD (FEV1 40%) complicated by cor pulmonale (right heart failure with marked leg edema). In hypoxaemic COPD with cor pulmonale, long-term oxygen therapy (used about 15 hours or more per day) is the intervention proven to prolong survival. The lead-in "most associated with increased survival" separates it from therapies that only improve symptoms.
why_wrong_block:
A. Heart-lung transplant is reserved for a highly selected few with end-stage disease; it is not the standard survival intervention in a 70-year-old.
B. Corticosteroids (inhaled or oral) reduce exacerbations but do not improve survival in COPD, and long-term oral steroids cause harm.
C. Pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise capacity, symptoms and quality of life and reduces admissions, but LTOT is the answer when survival is asked.
key_concept:
COPD interventions that improve survival:
  • Smoking cessation (most important overall)
  • LTOT in chronic hypoxaemia, especially with cor pulmonale
  • Vaccination
  • LTOT needs 2 ABGs: PaO2 <7.3 kPa, or 7.3 to 8 kPa with edema, pulmonary hypertension or polycythaemia
  • Rehab and inhalers: symptoms and quality of life, not mortality
exam_pearl: If smoking cessation is an option and the patient still smokes, it beats LTOT; in a cor pulmonale stem without it, LTOT wins.

stem: Diabetic pt with 6 months history of bilateral pain in PIP and MCP joints, also complains of dry eyes, investigations had high ESR and high CRP and (-ve) AntiSSA, asking about diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: bilateral pain in PIP and MCP joints
why_right: "6 months" of bilateral pain in the "PIP and MCP joints" with raised "ESR and CRP" is a symmetric inflammatory small-joint polyarthritis lasting more than 6 weeks, which is rheumatoid arthritis. The "dry eyes" with "negative anti-SSA" are best read as secondary sicca symptoms of RA rather than primary Sjögren syndrome.
why_wrong_block:
B. Primary Sjögren syndrome would be favoured by prominent dry eyes and mouth with positive anti-SSA (Ro) or anti-SSB (La); here anti-SSA is negative and the dominant problem is inflammatory arthritis.
C. Diabetic cheiroarthropathy causes painless stiffness and thick waxy skin with limited finger extension (prayer sign), with normal inflammatory markers; it is not a painful inflammatory synovitis.
D. Osteoarthritis involves DIP and PIP joints (Heberden and Bouchard nodes), spares MCPs, has brief morning stiffness and normal ESR and CRP.
key_concept:
Hand arthritis patterns:
  • RA: symmetric MCP, PIP, wrist; DIP spared; stiffness > 30 min; high ESR/CRP
  • OA: DIP and PIP, Heberden/Bouchard nodes, normal markers
  • Viral arthritis: RA-like but < 6 weeks
  • Primary Sjögren: sicca + anti-SSA/SSB positive
  • Diabetic cheiroarthropathy: painless stiffness, prayer sign
exam_pearl: Sicca symptoms with negative anti-SSA in a patient with symmetric MCP/PIP inflammatory arthritis = RA with secondary sicca, not primary Sjögren.

stem: A patient presents with periorbital eye swelling, hematuria, and hypertension. He had a sore throat 3 weeks ago. ASO titre: positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: periorbital eye swelling, hematuria, and hypertension
why_right: "Periorbital swelling, hematuria and hypertension" is a nephritic syndrome, and it follows a "sore throat 3 weeks ago" with a "positive ASO titre". This latent period of 1 to 3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis is classic for poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome in adults (heavy proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia), not post-infectious nephritic hematuria with hypertension.
B. IgA nephropathy gives hematuria within a few days of (or during) an upper respiratory infection; it would be right with a 1 to 2 day latency, not 3 weeks with a positive ASO.
key_concept:
Timing after infection separates the two classic causes.
  • PSGN: 1 to 3 weeks after throat (longer after skin) infection; positive ASO; low C3, normal C4
  • IgA nephropathy: hematuria within days of URTI; normal complement
  • Membranous: nephrotic, adults, anti-PLA2R
exam_pearl: Days after the sore throat = IgA nephropathy; weeks after = PSGN.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0681).

stem: 60 diagnosed AF, ask about medication to control ventricular rate:
why_right: The lead-in asks for a drug to "control ventricular rate" in AF with no heart failure, asthma or hypotension mentioned. First-line rate control is a beta blocker or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, and this recall's key is the beta blocker metoprolol, the usual default choice.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diltiazem is also a first-line rate-control agent; it is preferred when beta blockers are contraindicated (e.g. asthma) and must be avoided in heart failure with reduced EF. The key here favours the beta blocker.
B. Digoxin is reserved for AF with heart failure or sedentary patients, or as an add-on; it controls rate poorly during exertion and is not first line alone.
D. Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor for hypertension or heart failure; it has no effect on AV node conduction or ventricular rate.
key_concept:
AF management: stable patient = rate control first.
  • Rate control: beta blocker or non-DHP CCB (diltiazem, verapamil); target HR < 100 at rest
  • AF + heart failure (reduced EF): digoxin or beta blocker; avoid non-DHP CCBs
  • Asthma: prefer diltiazem/verapamil
  • Rhythm control: amiodarone
  • Unstable: synchronized cardioversion
exam_pearl: If the stem adds heart failure the answer flips to digoxin; if it adds asthma it flips to diltiazem.

stem: A Patient With Fatigue, Recurrent ureteric stones and bone pain, Ca: 3.50 mmol, Parathyroid adenoma: 2cm parathyroid adenoma. What's Most NEXT Appropriate Management? The Recall Didn't Mention: Polyuria, Polydipsia, CNS Symptoms (Only Mentioned Fatigue, No Lethargy Or Confusion)
highlight_terms_source: Recurrent ureteric stones and bone pain
why_right: This recall's key is bisphosphonate because of the markedly raised calcium ("Ca 3.50 mmol"), which is at the severe range: the reasoning is to lower calcium first (IV saline then IV bisphosphonate) before definitive surgery. The adenoma is already localized ("2 cm parathyroid adenoma"), so the next step chosen is control of the calcium level rather than more investigations.
why_wrong_block:
B. Calcimimetics (cinacalcet) lower PTH and calcium in patients who cannot or will not have surgery, or in secondary/tertiary disease; they act slowly and are not the acute step for a high calcium.
C. Increasing dietary calcium would worsen hypercalcemia; normal intake is advised in hyperparathyroidism, and restriction or supplements are not the treatment.
D. Parathyroidectomy is the definitive treatment and is clearly indicated here (symptomatic, renal stones, bone pain); it is the answer when the question asks for definitive or best management, with calcium stabilized first if severe.
key_concept:
Primary hyperparathyroidism: stabilize calcium if severe, then cure with surgery.
  • Severe or symptomatic hypercalcemia: IV normal saline, then IV bisphosphonate (calcitonin for rapid short-term effect)
  • Definitive: parathyroidectomy after sestamibi localization
  • Surgery indications: any symptoms, Ca ≥ 1 mg/dL above ULN, osteoporosis or fragility fracture, age < 50, stones/nephrocalcinosis or GFR < 60
  • Non-surgical candidates: cinacalcet, bisphosphonate for bone protection
exam_pearl: "Next" step with a very high calcium = lower it first; "definitive/best" management of an adenoma = parathyroidectomy.

stem: A Patient With Fatigue, Recurrent ureteric stones and bone pain, Ca: Not Known mmol, Parathyroid adenoma: 2cm parathyroid adenoma. What's Initial Next Step Management? The Recall Didn't Mention: Polyuria, Polydipsia, CNS Symptoms (Only Mentioned Fatigue, No Lethargy Or Confusion)
OptA: Calcitonin (I Am 100% Sure It Was NOT Calcimimetics)
highlight_terms_source: Recurrent ureteric stones and bone pain
key_concept:
Symptomatic PHPT = parathyroidectomy; acute drugs are only for crisis.
  • Surgical indications: any symptoms (stones, bone pain, fractures), Ca ≥1 mg/dL above upper normal, osteoporosis, age <50, renal involvement (stones, nephrocalcinosis, GFR <60)
  • Localize before surgery (sestamibi, neck US)
  • Crisis ladder: IV saline → IV bisphosphonate ± calcitonin → denosumab if refractory
  • Cinacalcet: for patients who cannot or will not have surgery
exam_pearl: Crisis features (confusion, vomiting, very high calcium) push toward IV fluids plus calcitonin first; stones and bone pain with a localized adenoma and no crisis push toward parathyroidectomy.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents to the ER with nausea, confusion, and muscle weakness. She has a history of breast cancer with bone metastases. Her serum calcium is 15.2 mg/dL (Normal: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL). Vitals: BP 130/80 mmHg, HR 90 bpm, no fever. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
why_right: Calcium 15.2 mg/dL with "confusion" and "muscle weakness" in a patient with "bone metastases" is severe, symptomatic hypercalcemia of malignancy. The true first step is aggressive IV normal saline, which is not offered; among the options, calcitonin is the fastest acting calcium lowering drug (works within hours), so it is the best initial pharmacologic step while IV bisphosphonate takes days to act.
why_wrong_block:
B. Surgery has no role in hypercalcemia from bone metastases; parathyroidectomy is for primary hyperparathyroidism with an adenoma.
C. Furosemide is not first line and can worsen dehydration (these patients are volume depleted); a loop diuretic is added only if fluid overload develops after rehydration.
D. Oral bisphosphonates are poorly absorbed and slow; severe hypercalcemia needs an IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid or pamidronate), and even that takes 2 to 4 days to work.
key_concept:
Severe or symptomatic hypercalcemia: hydrate first, then rapid plus sustained drugs.
  • Step 1: aggressive IV normal saline
  • Fast acting: calcitonin (hours, effect wanes in about 48 h due to tachyphylaxis)
  • Sustained: IV bisphosphonate (onset 2 to 4 days)
  • Refractory or renal impairment: denosumab; renal failure: dialysis
  • Lymphoma or granulomatous disease: steroids
  • Loop diuretic only for volume overload
exam_pearl: If IV saline is an option, it beats calcitonin as the initial step; without it, pick calcitonin over oral bisphosphonate or furosemide.

stem: Patient came with 12 hours of history of lower limb weakness, all vitals within normal range. Coagulation profile is normal and platelet normal (I missed numbers). Imaging showed: small to moderate ischemic core, proximal anterior circulation occlusion. What's the most appropriate management?
key_concept:
Ischemic stroke reperfusion depends on time + vessel + core.
  • ≤4.5 h, no contraindication: IV thrombolysis
  • ≤4.5 h + large vessel occlusion: tPA then thrombectomy
  • 6 to 24 h + LVO + small core / mismatch: thrombectomy alone
  • Unknown onset: MRI DWI/FLAIR mismatch decides tPA
  • Deficit resolved: no reperfusion, start secondary prevention (antiplatelet, statin, BP, workup)
exam_pearl: The same stem flips to Observe if the weakness has resolved (see the paired card).
compiler_note:
⚠ Image audit: The compiler marked this answer tentatively ('??' / 'not sure' / needs re-correction) — see the compiler note.
Compiler note: No option highlighted; B carries '??'. Compiler's note under 496: If weakness resolve = observe; if weakness not resolve = Embolectomy.

stem: Patient came with 12 hours of history of lower limb weakness That Has Resolved, all vitals within normal range. Coagulation profile is normal and platelet normal (I missed numbers). Imaging showed: small to moderate ischemic core, Proximal anterior circulation occlusion. What's the most appropriate management?
key_concept:
Resolved deficit = no reperfusion; persisting deficit with LVO = thrombectomy.
  • ≤4.5 h: IV thrombolysis if deficit persists
  • 6 to 24 h + LVO + small core: mechanical thrombectomy
  • Symptoms resolved: observe/monitor, antiplatelet, risk factor control
  • Watch for re-deterioration: a persistent occlusion can fluctuate, so reassess if weakness returns
exam_pearl: Read the word "resolved": present weakness points to embolectomy, resolved weakness points to observation.

stem: 78-year-old male presented with change level of consciousness and fever, lumbar puncture was done showed CF gram +ve bacilli catalase positive. How will you treat?
why_right: CSF showing "gram +ve bacilli" that are "catalase positive" identifies Listeria monocytogenes, and a 78 year old (age over 50) is a classic Listeria host. Once the LP result names the organism, you treat the organism rather than give empirical cover; Listeria is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins, so ampicillin is the drug of choice (often with gentamicin for synergy).
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin plus steroid is empirical cover for pneumococcus and meningococcus in younger adults; it misses Listeria entirely, and dexamethasone is not beneficial in Listeria meningitis.
B. Ceftriaxone plus ampicillin plus vancomycin is the correct empirical regimen for meningitis in patients over 50 before the organism is known; here the Gram stain already shows Listeria, so targeted ampicillin is the answer.
C. Same three drugs as option B in a different order: right as empirical therapy in an older adult with unknown organism, but not once Gram positive, catalase positive bacilli are reported.
key_concept:
Gram positive bacilli in CSF (catalase positive) = Listeria = ampicillin.
  • Neonates: ampicillin + gentamicin (or cefotaxime) empirically
  • Age 2 months to 50: ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone
  • Age over 50 or immunocompromised: add ampicillin for Listeria
  • Organism known from LP: treat the organism, not empirically
  • Cephalosporins never cover Listeria
exam_pearl: If the stem gave no Gram stain, the 78 year old would get ceftriaxone + vancomycin + ampicillin; the reported bacilli turn it into ampicillin alone.

stem: Patient presents with epigastric pain that worsens after eating. She has a history of NSAID use. Endoscopy reveals a duodenal ulcer. What is the next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: epigastric pain that worsens after eating
why_right: The decisive clue is "history of NSAID use" with an endoscopically proven "duodenal ulcer": this is an NSAID induced ulcer, so management is to stop the NSAID and heal the ulcer with a PPI. A PPI is the most effective acid suppressant and the backbone of every ulcer treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Elective surgery is reserved for complications (perforation, refractory bleeding, obstruction) or truly refractory ulcers, none of which are present.
B. H. pylori eradication is right when the ulcer is H. pylori related (no NSAID history, positive test; see the paired card). H. pylori should still be tested in any ulcer, but antibiotics are given only if positive, and with a clear NSAID cause the first treatment is PPI.
D. Diet change and antacids give symptom relief only and do not heal a proven ulcer.
key_concept:
Proven peptic ulcer: remove the cause and give PPI.
  • NSAID ulcer: stop NSAID + PPI (if NSAID must continue, keep PPI cover)
  • No NSAID: H. pylori is the main cause, eradicate (PPI based regimen; bismuth quadruple where clarithromycin resistance is high)

stem: A 55-year-old male smoker presents to the Emergency Room with a sudden onset of retrosternal chest pain radiating to the neck. His systemic examination is unremarkable. ECG: ST-segment depression in II, III, and aVE. Which of the following is the most considerable risk factor?

exam_pearl: "Most considerable" risk factor = age; "most important modifiable" = smoking.

stem: Clear question about patient has potassium 6 what is the finding in ECG?
why_right: A potassium of 6 mmol/L is hyperkalemia, and the peaked (tall, tented) T wave is its earliest and most classic ECG sign. It reflects faster ventricular repolarization as extracellular potassium rises. The other options describe changes in the opposite direction or belong to other conditions.
why_wrong_block:
B. Peaked P waves (P pulmonale) mean right atrial enlargement. In hyperkalemia the P wave flattens and eventually disappears.
C. Hyperkalemia prolongs the PR interval. A short PR points to pre-excitation such as WPW.
D. Hyperkalemia widens the QRS complex as it worsens; it never narrows it.
key_concept:
Hyperkalemia ECG progresses in a predictable order as potassium rises.
  • 1st: peaked T waves
  • 2nd: PR prolongation, then flattened or absent P waves
  • 3rd: QRS widening
  • 4th: sine wave pattern, then VF or asystole
  • Any ECG change: give IV calcium gluconate first to stabilize the myocardium
exam_pearl: Hypokalemia is the mirror image: flattened T waves and U waves; do not mix up the two.

stem: A Patient Presents With Nausea And Vomiting For 3 Days And Develops Muscle Weakness. Labs Show Potassium Level Of 2.9 Mmol/L. What Is The Most Appropriate Management?
why_right: Potassium 2.9 mmol/L with muscle weakness is symptomatic hypokalemia, and 3 days of vomiting mean oral replacement will not be kept down, so potassium must go intravenously. Vomiting also leaves the patient volume depleted with a chloride responsive metabolic alkalosis, so potassium is given diluted in IV normal saline, which corrects the volume, chloride and potassium deficits together.

A. Observation is unsafe in symptomatic hypokalemia below 3 mmol/L because of the arrhythmia and paralysis risk.
B. Oral KCl is preferred for asymptomatic mild to moderate hypokalemia when the patient can take and keep down tablets; this patient is symptomatic and vomiting.
C. IV KCl alone ignores the volume depletion from vomiting, and potassium is never pushed undiluted; it is given within IV fluid at a controlled rate, which is what D describes.
key_concept:

  • Severe (below about 2.5), symptomatic, ECG changes or vomiting: IV potassium
  • Vomiting: give it in saline to fix volume and alkalosis
  • Give IV K in saline, not dextrose (dextrose drives K into cells)
  • Refractory hypokalemia: check and replace magnesium
exam_pearl: Hypokalemia that will not correct despite adequate replacement means hypomagnesemia until proven otherwise.

stem: Female patient aged 45 medically free no HTN or DM. BMI 38. She has a positive family history of premature cardiac death. LDL ~3.47 (higher than normal range) Whats the best counseling for her/lower her cardiovascular risk?
highlight_terms_source: positive family history of premature cardiac death
why_right: She is a 45-year-old woman with no hypertension and no diabetes and an LDL of about 3.47 mmol/L, far below the 4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL) threshold that mandates high-intensity statin. She has no clinical ASCVD, so this is primary prevention where her 10-year risk is likely low. Her main modifiable problem is BMI 38, so lifestyle modification (diet, exercise, weight loss) is the best counseling; the family history is a risk enhancer that matters if her calculated risk is borderline or intermediate.
why_wrong_block: A. High-intensity statin is for clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL), or high-risk diabetics; a normotensive non-diabetic with LDL 3.47 does not meet these.
key_concept:
Statin benefit groups (age >21):
  • Clinical ASCVD: high-intensity statin
  • LDL ≥190 mg/dL (≈4.9 mmol/L): high-intensity statin
  • Diabetes, 40 to 75 y, LDL 70 to 189: moderate (high if multiple risk factors or 10-y risk ≥20%)
  • No diabetes, 40 to 75 y, LDL 70 to 189, 10-y risk ≥7.5%: moderate to high
  • Everyone else: lifestyle first; family history is a risk enhancer, not an automatic statin trigger
exam_pearl: Mildly raised LDL plus obesity and no HTN/DM = lifestyle first; the LDL must reach ≈4.9 mmol/L before statin is automatic.

stem: Male Patient, 45 Years Old, Hypertensive And Smoker For 20 Years. Lipid Profile Shows: LDL 4.3, Total Cholesterol 6.1, Triglycerides Normal. What Is The Best Preventive Counseling?
OptB: Lifestyle Modifications And Recheck Lipid After 3 Months
OptC: Give Aspirin No Moderate Intensity Statin
why_right: This 45-year-old man has stacked risk factors: hypertension, 20 years of smoking, LDL 4.3 and total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/L. That combination puts his 10-year ASCVD risk in the range where statin therapy is recommended, so this recall's key is to start a statin now rather than wait. Lifestyle change and smoking cessation are added on top, not used as a substitute.
why_wrong_block:
B. Lifestyle alone with a 3-month recheck suits a low-risk person with mildly raised LDL (like a young normotensive non-smoker); with HTN plus heavy smoking, delaying statin is not appropriate.
C. Aspirin is not routine for primary prevention because bleeding risk offsets the benefit, and withholding a statin removes the key preventive drug.
key_concept:
Primary prevention statin decision = LDL level + 10-year ASCVD risk.
  • LDL ≥190 mg/dL (≈4.9 mmol/L) or clinical ASCVD: high-intensity statin
  • Age 40 to 75, LDL 70 to 189, risk ≥7.5%: moderate to high intensity
  • Several risk factors (HTN, smoking) push the risk up
  • Always add lifestyle and smoking cessation
  • Aspirin: not routine in primary prevention
exam_pearl: Same LDL range as a low-risk patient, but HTN plus long smoking history flips the answer from lifestyle to statin.

stem: A patient presents with dull chest pain that is not related to activity. The pain is more prominent after spicy meals or emotional stress and increases with lying flat. [Hb Not Mentioned] How to establish the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: chest pain that is not related to activity
why_right: Non-exertional chest pain made worse by spicy meals and lying flat is typical of GERD. In this version no anemia or other alarm feature is given, so there is no reason for endoscopy first. Ambulatory 24-hour pH monitoring is the test that objectively confirms reflux as the cause of the symptoms.
why_wrong_block:
A. Barium swallow assesses structure and motility in dysphagia (strictures, rings, achalasia); it does not confirm acid reflux.
B. Endoscopy is for alarm features (anemia, dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, older age) or refractory symptoms; none is given here (compare the Hb 110 version, where endoscopy is the answer).
C. Manometry diagnoses motility disorders (achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm with dysphagia) and is done before fundoplication, not to diagnose reflux.
key_concept:
Reflux-type chest pain: alarm features pick the test.
  • No alarm features: clinical diagnosis/PPI trial; to objectively confirm GERD: 24 h pH (impedance) monitoring
  • Alarm features (anemia, dysphagia, weight loss, GI bleeding): endoscopy first
  • Refractory GERD, normal endoscopy: pH monitoring
  • Refractory GERD with esophagitis: manometry, then fundoplication
  • Dysphagia to liquids and solids: barium swallow, then manometry
exam_pearl: Twin recall: same stem with Hb 110 (anemia = alarm feature) changes the answer to endoscopy.

stem: A patient presents with dull chest pain that is not related to activity. The pain is more prominent after spicy meals or emotional stress and increases with lying flat. [Hb 110] How to establish the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: chest pain that is not related to activity
why_right: The pain pattern (worse with spicy meals and lying flat, unrelated to exertion) suggests reflux or peptic disease, but this version gives Hb 110, i.e. anemia. Anemia is an alarm feature suggesting mucosal blood loss (esophagitis, ulcer, malignancy), so upper endoscopy is needed to see the mucosa and biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Barium swallow is for dysphagia work-up or when endoscopy is contraindicated or unavailable; it cannot biopsy or reliably show a bleeding lesion.
C. Manometry is for motility disorders (achalasia, esophageal spasm) or before fundoplication, not for anemia with reflux symptoms.
D. pH monitoring confirms reflux when there are NO alarm features or when endoscopy is normal (the Hb-not-mentioned version); anemia needs direct visualization first.
key_concept:
Alarm features mean endoscopy first.
  • Anemia / iron deficiency
  • Dysphagia or odynophagia
  • Weight loss
  • GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena, isolated high urea)
  • Older age with new symptoms
  • Persistent vomiting
exam_pearl: Same stem without Hb = pH monitoring; add Hb 110 = endoscopy.

stem: A male has readings of high blood pressure. he doesn't exercise, high salt intake, and has stressful job. bp 138/88 (or 98 not sure) Na 160 other labs normal what is the INITIAL approach to manage this patient?
OptB: lower salt intake and enhance physical activity
OptC: advice to monitor bp and record the readings (something like that)
why_right: He has repeated raised readings around 138/88 with clear lifestyle drivers (no exercise, high salt intake, stress) and no target organ damage. At this level the INITIAL management is lifestyle modification: reduce salt, increase physical activity, manage weight and stress. Drugs are added only if BP stays above target despite lifestyle change or if overall cardiovascular risk is high.
why_wrong_block:
A. Immediate drug therapy is for BP ≥160/100, target organ damage, or high cardiovascular risk; 138/88 without these starts with lifestyle change.
C. Home or ambulatory monitoring is right to CONFIRM a single raised office reading (especially near 140/90); here readings are already raised and lifestyle advice is indicated regardless.
key_concept:
Raised BP: confirm, then lifestyle first, drugs by level and risk.
  • Single office reading: confirm with home/ambulatory BP
  • High-normal / stage 1 without target organ damage: lifestyle first
  • Stage 1 not responding: add a first-line drug (ACEi/ARB, CCB, thiazide)
  • ≥160/100 or target organ damage: start drugs now (with lifestyle)
  • Lifestyle: salt restriction, exercise, weight loss, limit alcohol
exam_pearl: The serum Na of 160 is almost certainly a recall artifact; dietary salt does not cause marked hypernatremia, so do not let it drive the answer.

stem: Old male came to the travel clinic. He has a 14 hour flight and his friend told him about DVT And he came for advice on how to prevent it?
key_concept:
Long-haul flight VTE prevention is graded by risk.
  • All travelers: mobilize, calf exercises, aisle seat, hydration
  • Increased risk: add properly fitted below-knee compression stockings
  • Very high risk: consider prophylactic LMWH, individualized
  • Aspirin is not recommended for travel VTE prevention
exam_pearl: Age alone does not justify an anticoagulant for a flight; the answer climbs the ladder only with added risk factors.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No option marked.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 70 years old Came to er after 12h complain of symptoms with rt side weakness. Ct showed: posterior artery occlusion with mild to moderate ischemic core Management?
why_right: He presents at 12 hours, beyond the 4.5-hour IV thrombolysis window, with a large-vessel occlusion and only a mild-to-moderate ischemic core, meaning salvageable brain remains. Mechanical thrombectomy is indicated for selected large-vessel occlusions up to 24 hours from last known well, for anterior circulation and, from recent trials, basilar (posterior) occlusion too. The other version of this recall describes a proximal anterior circulation occlusion; the management is the same.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV tPA is limited to 4.5 hours from onset (or last known well); at 12 hours it adds bleeding risk without proven benefit.
B. Observation (supportive care, antiplatelet) fits when there is no vessel to open or the tissue is already fully infarcted with no salvageable brain; here an occluded large vessel with a mild-to-moderate core still has tissue to save.
D. Bridging tPA plus thrombectomy is used when the patient arrives within 4.5 hours; at 12 hours only thrombectomy is given.
key_concept:
Acute ischemic stroke: time and vessel decide.
  • Step 1: glucose, then noncontrast CT to exclude bleed
  • ≤4.5 h, no contraindication: IV thrombolysis
  • LVO within 4.5 h: tPA plus thrombectomy
  • LVO 6 to 24 h with small/moderate core on imaging: thrombectomy alone
  • Large core within 24 h: thrombectomy now considered in selected patients (recent trials)
  • No LVO and outside 4.5 h: supportive care, aspirin within 24 to 48 h
exam_pearl: Past 4.5 hours, tPA drops out, but thrombectomy stays on the table up to 24 hours if the core is not large.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q): right sided weakness that started 12 hours ago, proximal anterior circulation occlusion, moderate size infarct core; options A- tPA, B- Mechanical thrombectomy (highlighted), C- Observation, D- tPA and mechanical thrombectomy.

stem: 68 years old came to the er with 3 days history of bilateral leg weakness and brisk movements reflexes in both legs, with urine retention and inability to walk and sensory level of T10. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: Bilateral leg weakness with brisk reflexes (upper motor neuron), urinary retention and a sensory level at T10 localizes to the thoracic spinal cord. In a 68-year-old with a 3-day course, the most likely cause is spinal cord compression (often metastatic epidural disease or degenerative/disc), which needs urgent whole-spine MRI and steroids.
why_wrong_block:
A. Transverse myelitis also gives a sensory level, UMN signs and bladder involvement, but it typically affects younger patients, often after infection or with MS/NMO, and MRI shows no compressive lesion.
B. GBS is an ascending polyneuropathy with areflexia and no sensory level; brisk reflexes exclude it.
C. Cauda equina is a lower motor neuron root lesion below L1: reduced or absent reflexes, saddle anesthesia and back pain, not hyperreflexia with a T10 level.
key_concept:
Leg weakness plus bladder: localize first.
  • Sensory level + UMN signs + bladder: spinal cord (myelopathy)
  • Older patient, acute/subacute: compression (metastases, disc, abscess) until MRI proves otherwise
  • Younger, post-infectious, no compressive lesion: transverse myelitis
  • Areflexia, ascending, no sensory level: GBS
  • LMN signs, saddle anesthesia: cauda equina
  • Work-up: urgent whole-spine MRI; give dexamethasone if malignancy suspected
exam_pearl: Sensory level plus brisk reflexes means cord, not roots or nerves; age then tips compression over myelitis.

stem: Patient Known case of UC, Presented with severe Bloody diarrhea, Patient is very sick. What to Add after IV fluid?
why_right: A known UC patient with "severe bloody diarrhea" who is "very sick" has acute severe ulcerative colitis (frequent bloody stools plus systemic toxicity). After resuscitation with IV fluids, the next step is IV corticosteroids, and IV methylprednisolone (or IV hydrocortisone) is the standard first line induction agent. IV route is chosen because a toxic patient needs reliable, rapid, high dose steroid effect.
why_wrong_block:
A. Azathioprine is a slow acting steroid sparing agent used for maintenance of remission; it takes weeks to work and has no role in rescuing an acute severe flare.
C. Oral prednisone is used for moderate flares in an outpatient who is not toxic; a very sick patient with severe bloody diarrhea needs IV steroids.
key_concept:
Acute severe UC: IV fluids then IV steroids, reassess at day 3.
  • Definition: 6 or more bloody stools/day PLUS systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, anemia, raised ESR/CRP)
  • First line: IV methylprednisolone or IV hydrocortisone
  • Also: VTE prophylaxis, stool tests to exclude C. difficile
  • No response at about day 3: rescue with infliximab or ciclosporin
  • Failure of rescue, toxic megacolon or perforation: colectomy
  • Azathioprine and 5-ASA: maintenance, not rescue
exam_pearl: Mild to moderate flare = oral steroid or 5-ASA; "very sick" or toxic = admit and give IV steroid.

stem: A patient with pneumonia is agitated, pH 7.1, and PaO₂ 7 kPa. What is the best management?
why_right: This patient has severe respiratory failure from pneumonia: profound hypoxemia ("PaO2 7 kPa"), severe acidemia ("pH 7.1") and he is "agitated". Altered mental status and agitation mean he cannot protect his airway or tolerate a mask, and the degree of acidosis predicts failure of non-invasive support, so controlled (elective) intubation and mechanical ventilation is the safest step.
why_wrong_block: B. BiPAP needs an alert, cooperative patient who can protect the airway; it is best for hypercapnic COPD exacerbations with moderate acidosis. An agitated patient with pH 7.1 and severe hypoxemic pneumonia is a contraindication and delaying intubation worsens outcome.
key_concept:
NIV vs intubation: decide on mental status, airway protection and severity.
  • NIV (BiPAP): alert, cooperative, hypercapnic (classically COPD), moderate acidosis
  • Intubate: agitated, confused or drowsy, cannot protect airway, copious secretions
  • Intubate: severe acidosis, refractory hypoxemia, hemodynamic instability
  • Intubate: NIV trial failing or worsening ABG
exam_pearl: Any altered consciousness (agitated, drowsy, confused) with respiratory failure pushes the answer from NIV to intubation.

stem: A patient had an upper respiratory tract infection 5 days ago. Suddenly, he developed loss of consciousness and difficulty breathing. He is currently intubated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: upper respiratory tract infection 5 days ago
why_right: This recall's key is pulmonary edema: a previously well patient with an "upper respiratory tract infection 5 days ago" who suddenly deteriorates with "difficulty breathing" and reduced consciousness needing intubation fits an acute lung injury picture, where infection triggers non-cardiogenic (ARDS type) pulmonary edema, or less often viral myocarditis causes cardiogenic edema. Hypoxemia leads to decreased consciousness and respiratory failure, explaining the intubation. Per the compiler's note, the different recall versions (no ABG, normal CO2, high CO2) were all keyed to pulmonary edema, since CO2 is low early and rises as the patient tires.
why_wrong_block:
B. Myasthenia gravis causes fluctuating fatigable weakness (ptosis, diplopia, bulbar signs) and can crisis after infection, but nothing here suggests known MG or weakness; post infection ascending weakness would point to GBS instead.
C. COPD is a chronic disease of older smokers with prior symptoms; it is not a sudden new diagnosis after a URTI, although a URTI can trigger an exacerbation in a known COPD patient.
D. Drug overdose causes reduced consciousness with hypoventilation, but there is no history of ingestion and the preceding URTI is the key link offered by the stem.
key_concept:
Sudden respiratory failure days after a viral infection: think lung injury (ARDS type pulmonary edema).
  • ARDS: acute onset (within 1 week of insult), bilateral infiltrates, hypoxemia, not explained by heart failure
  • Common triggers: pneumonia (viral or bacterial), sepsis, aspiration
  • Viral myocarditis: cardiogenic pulmonary edema after a viral illness
  • Post infection weakness with areflexia: GBS
  • Fatigable weakness, ptosis, diplopia: MG
exam_pearl: Post URTI + respiratory failure with NO weakness pattern = lung (edema/ARDS); post URTI + ascending weakness and areflexia = GBS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall 1: same scenario + ABG not mentioned; Recall 2: ABG showing normal CO2; Recall 3: ABG showing high CO2. All are pulmonary edema; MG is not even near close to correct (P-edema starts low CO2 if mild, then normal CO2, then becomes high CO2). Screenshot version (ICU, URTI 5 days ago worsening daily, decreased consciousness) gives Answer: A. Classical case of Hamman Rich syndrome (non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema).

stem: A 45-year-old man presented to the Emergency Room with palpitations. Initially, he was conscious and oriented. His vital signs were as shown. After some time, he became less responsive, and his blood pressure dropped to 80/45 mmHg (see report). ECG: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?
why_right: The decisive change is instability: the patient became "less responsive" and his BP fell to 80/45 mmHg during SVT. Any tachyarrhythmia with hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest pain or acute heart failure is treated with immediate synchronized cardioversion, not drugs or vagal maneuvers.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pacing treats symptomatic bradyarrhythmias (e.g. high grade AV block after atropine fails), not a tachyarrhythmia like SVT.
C. Rate control drugs belong to the stable pathway after vagal maneuvers and adenosine; a beta blocker can deepen hypotension in an unstable patient.
D. Ablation is elective definitive therapy for recurrent symptomatic SVT (or WPW failing drugs), never an emergency treatment for a crashing patient.
key_concept:
In any tachyarrhythmia, stability decides the path first.
  • Unstable (hypotension, reduced consciousness, shock, ischemic pain, acute HF): synchronized cardioversion
  • Stable narrow complex SVT: vagal maneuvers first
  • Then IV adenosine if vagal maneuvers fail
  • Then beta blocker or non dihydropyridine CCB
  • Recurrent symptomatic SVT long term: radiofrequency ablation
exam_pearl: The same SVT with a normal BP and full consciousness flips the answer to vagal maneuvers (carotid sinus massage).

stem: Patient is positive for TB, which TB medication causes high uric acid?
why_right: Pyrazinamide reduces renal excretion of uric acid, so "high uric acid" in a patient on anti-TB therapy points to it. Hyperuricemia is common and often asymptomatic, but it can precipitate gout. Pyrazinamide is also one of the hepatotoxic first line drugs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy (pyridoxine depletion, prevented by vitamin B6) and hepatitis, not hyperuricemia.
B. Rifampicin causes orange red body fluids, hepatotoxicity and many drug interactions as an enzyme inducer, not hyperuricemia.
C. Ethambutol causes optic neuritis (reduced acuity, red green color blindness); hyperuricemia is reported but is the classic association of pyrazinamide.
key_concept:
Anti-TB drug side effects (RIPE):
  • Rifampicin: orange secretions, enzyme inducer (interactions), hepatitis
  • Isoniazid: peripheral neuropathy (give B6), hepatitis
  • Pyrazinamide: hyperuricemia and gout, hepatitis
  • Ethambutol: optic neuritis, red green color loss (E for Eye)
exam_pearl: Uric acid or gout on TB drugs = Pyrazinamide; vision change = Ethambutol; numbness = Isoniazid.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot version: 45-year-old man started on 4 anti-TB drugs 2 months ago; routine follow up shows hyperuricemia (uric acid 600, normal 200-410 male). What anti-TB drug is responsible? Marked **D. Pyrazinamide.

stem: A patient received blood transfusions before 12 years and developed symptoms of chronic hepatitis. HBV antibodies positive HBV antigen negative HCV antibodies positive Hepatitis C RNA = 1.5 million Which type of chronic hepatitis does this patient have?
why_right: The decisive result is "Hepatitis C RNA = 1.5 million": a positive HCV antibody plus detectable HCV RNA confirms active (viremic) HCV infection, and with symptoms years after a blood transfusion this is chronic hepatitis C. The hepatitis B results (antibody positive, antigen negative) mean past cleared infection or vaccination, not active hepatitis B.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hepatitis A is fecal oral, acute and self limiting and never becomes chronic; no HAV marker is given.
B. Chronic hepatitis B requires HBsAg positive for more than 6 months; here HBV antigen is negative and only antibody is positive, which indicates immunity (recovery or vaccination).
D. Hepatitis D is a defective virus that needs HBsAg to replicate, so it cannot exist when HBV antigen is negative.
key_concept:
Antibody tells exposure; antigen or RNA tells active infection.
  • Anti-HCV positive + HCV RNA positive: active HCV (chronic if beyond 6 months)
  • Anti-HCV positive + HCV RNA negative: cleared infection or false positive
  • HBsAg positive beyond 6 months: chronic HBV
  • Anti-HBs positive, HBsAg negative: immune (recovered or vaccinated)
  • HDV needs HBsAg; HAV never chronic
exam_pearl: An earlier, shorter recall gave only "HBV antibodies positive" and was marked B; antibody alone does not mean active disease, the RNA result makes it C.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Three versions in this block: (1) 4th February recall 'pt transfer blood before 12 years; s/s of chronic hepatitis; Hbv antibodies positive' with B highlighted; (2) Q: HBV antibodies positive, HBV antigen negative, HCV antibodies positive, '100% sure Hbc was not mentioned' (no mark); (3) fullest Q: adds Hepatitis C RNA = 1.5 million, with C highlighted.
Other marked answers: Earlier typed recall (4th February; only 'Hbv antibodies positive' given): B

stem: A 22-year-old man is evaluated for a 2-day history of dysuria and urethral discharge. He had recent sexual activity with a new female partner. He is afebrile, and his examination is unremarkable (see report). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
why_right: "Dysuria and urethral discharge" after a "new female partner" in an afebrile young man is urethritis; the accompanying report in this recall showed Chlamydia trachomatis. This recall's key is azithromycin, the classic exam answer for chlamydial urethritis (single oral dose, good adherence).
why_wrong_block:
A. Gentamycin: an aminoglycoside used for gram negative sepsis or pyelonephritis; it is not first line for chlamydia, which is intracellular.
C. Ceftriaxone: the drug for gonorrhea; it has no activity against intracellular Chlamydia, so it would be right if the report showed Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gram negative intracellular diplococci).
D. Nitrofurantoin: for uncomplicated cystitis in women; it does not treat sexually transmitted urethritis.
key_concept:
Urethritis in a sexually active man: identify the organism and treat partners.
  • Chlamydia: doxycycline 7 days (current preferred) or azithromycin single dose
  • Gonorrhea: ceftriaxone IM
  • Organism unknown: cover both (ceftriaxone plus anti-chlamydial)
  • Diagnosis: NAAT on urethral swab or first-void urine
  • Treat sexual partners
exam_pearl: Gram negative diplococci in the report = ceftriaxone; chlamydia only = azithromycin/doxycycline.

stem: A 55 years old man newly diagnosed with DM2 Started on Metformin 1000 BID and gliclazide or glyburide, after 6 months of treatment Urea: Normal Fasting 6.8 ( normal <6.5 ) A1C was 5.8 (normal 4.7-5.6) What is the next step?
OptD: Inform him he is at High cardiovascular risk
why_right: After 6 months on metformin plus a sulfonylurea, his "A1C was 5.8" which is well below the usual target of less than 7%, and his renal marker is normal. Glycemic control is achieved, so no intensification is needed and reassurance with continued follow up is the answer. The slightly raised fasting value (6.8) is a single reading and is outweighed by the HbA1c.
why_wrong_block:
B. Increasing the dose is for HbA1c above target; with HbA1c 5.8 it would only raise the risk of hypoglycemia, especially with gliclazide or glyburide.
C. Insulin is added when HbA1c remains above target despite oral agents or with very high HbA1c or catabolic symptoms; none apply here.
D. Diabetes does raise cardiovascular risk, but this statement does not answer the question asked, which is how to act on his glycemic results; risk factor management is part of routine care, not the next step for an at target HbA1c.
key_concept:
HbA1c drives the decision: at target = no change.
  • General target: HbA1c less than 7%
  • At or below target: continue, reassure, follow up
  • Above target on maximal dual therapy: add a third agent or insulin
  • Very low HbA1c on a sulfonylurea: watch for hypoglycemia
exam_pearl: Do not be distracted by a mildly high single fasting glucose; HbA1c at target means no escalation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): Patient in 50s at follow up clinic k/c of DM on metformin 500 mg BID and gliclazide, HbA1c 5.8 (normal 5.6); options Reassure / Increase metformin and gliclazide dose / Add insulin / Tell him he is at high risk for cardiovascular disease; Reassure highlighted.

stem: year-old woman known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus just returned from Makkah. She complains of fever, lethargy, and headache. She has no cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or skin rash. Examination reveals a drowsy patient with positive neck stiffness (see report). Lumbar puncture: Low glucose, markedly increased protein, WBC 9000 with predominantly neutrophils. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to start?
highlight_terms_source: Low glucose, markedly increased protein, WBC 9000 with predominantly neutrophils
why_right: Fever, drowsiness and neck stiffness with CSF showing low glucose, markedly raised protein and a neutrophil predominant WBC is bacterial meningitis. In an adult under 50, empiric therapy is a third generation cephalosporin plus vancomycin, keyed here as ceftriaxone and vancomycin; ceftriaxone also covers meningococcus, relevant after a trip to Makkah, and vancomycin covers resistant pneumococcus.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cefotaxime and vancomycin: pharmacologically similar coverage, but the standard keyed adult regimen uses ceftriaxone; cefotaxime is mainly favoured in neonates.
B. Ampicillin and cefotaxime: the neonatal regimen covering Listeria and Gram negatives; it lacks vancomycin for resistant pneumococcus.
D. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin: the community acquired pneumonia combination for atypicals; azithromycin has no role in meningitis.
key_concept:
Empiric bacterial meningitis therapy by age:
  • Neonate: ampicillin + cefotaxime (or gentamicin)
  • Child and adult under 50: ceftriaxone + vancomycin
  • Over 50, pregnant or immunocompromised: add ampicillin for Listeria
  • Dexamethasone with or just before the first antibiotic dose in suspected pneumococcal meningitis
  • Hajj or Umrah: think Neisseria meningitidis
exam_pearl: Neutrophils + low glucose = bacterial; lymphocytes + normal glucose = viral; lymphocytes + low glucose = TB or fungal.

stem: A 60-year-old man known to have hypertension and post aortic valve replacement on lisinopril 20 mg. amlodipine 5 mg and warfarin 3 mg once daily. He was admitted to the hospital with history of productive cough and shortness of breath, and was found to have positive acid fast bacilli (AFB) in sputum. First line four anti-TB drugs were started. Which’s of the following medications needs to be adjusted?
why_right: This recall's key is amlodipine. The first line regimen contains rifampicin, a potent liver enzyme (CYP3A4) inducer, and amlodipine is metabolised by CYP3A4, so its levels fall and blood pressure control may be lost; the dose may need increasing. The compiler notes that warfarin, the classic drug affected in this exact scenario, was not among the recalled options, so amlodipine is the remaining interacting drug.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lisinopril is excreted unchanged by the kidneys and is not metabolised by liver enzymes, so rifampicin does not meaningfully change its level.
C. This option was not recalled (blank); in the original version of this question the answer is that warfarin needs to be increased.
D. Rifampin is the cause of the interaction, not the drug to adjust; anti-TB drug doses are weight based and are not changed because of his antihypertensives.
key_concept:
Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer: it LOWERS levels of co-prescribed drugs.
  • Warfarin: INR falls, increase dose and monitor INR closely (critical after valve replacement)
  • CYP3A4 substrates (e.g. amlodipine, other calcium channel blockers): reduced effect
  • Oral contraceptives: reduced efficacy, use another method
  • Steroids and many antiretrovirals also affected
  • Renally cleared drugs (lisinopril): little effect
exam_pearl: Post valve replacement on warfarin + TB therapy = warfarin needs increasing; if warfarin is missing from the options, look for the other hepatically metabolised drug.
compiler_note: Compiler note: No Warfarin (warfarin was not among the options).

stem: A 30-year-old woman with bronchial asthma developed worsening dyspnea and cough following paint inhalation from neighborhood apartment. On examination, she is in respiratory distress, cannot complete a sentence and cyanosed. Chest auscultation revealed reduced breath sounds in both sides with short inspiratory and exploratory rhonchi (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 130 /min Respiratory rate 20 /min Oxygen saturation 85 % Test Result Normal Values ABG HCO3- 24 22-28 mmol/L ABG PCO2 7.8 4.7-6.0 kPa pH 7.3 7.36-7.45 ABG PO2 7.5 10.6-14.2 kPa Which of the following is the best immediate action in management?
OptD: Nasal continuous positive airway pressure ventilation
highlight_terms_source: cannot complete a sentence and cyanosed
why_right: This is life threatening asthma with respiratory failure: she is "cyanosed", "cannot complete a sentence", SpO2 85%, PaO2 7.5 kPa (hypoxemia) and, critically, PaCO2 7.8 kPa with pH 7.3. In acute asthma the CO2 should be low from hyperventilation, so a raised CO2 with acidosis signals exhaustion and impending arrest. The best immediate action is intubation and mechanical ventilation.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV magnesium is given in acute severe asthma not responding to bronchodilators and steroids, before the patient reaches hypercapnic failure; with rising CO2 and cyanosis it is too slow to be the immediate action.
B. IV aminophylline is a late, rarely used add on with a narrow therapeutic window and arrhythmia risk; it does not correct established respiratory failure.
D. CPAP or NIV is not recommended in acute asthma with hypercapnic failure; it delays definitive airway control and may worsen air trapping.
key_concept:
Acute asthma ladder: O2, SABA, ipratropium, systemic steroid, then IV magnesium, then ICU and intubation.
  • Severe: cannot complete sentences, RR and HR high
  • Life threatening: SpO2 below 92%, cyanosis, silent chest, exhaustion, confusion
  • Near fatal: raised PaCO2 or need for ventilation
  • Normal or high CO2 in asthma = tiring, escalate
exam_pearl: Hypercapnia in asthma is an ominous sign, unlike COPD where an alert hypercapnic patient may get NIV.

stem: A 62-year-old woman known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and ischemic stroke 1 month ago, presented to the Emergency Room complaining of central stabbing continuous chest pain for 3 hours. She denied any dyspnea, palpitation, or change in consciousness. The patient is taking insulin, lisinopril, metoprolol, lipitor, and aspirin. Examination revealed she is in pain. She was started on oxygen, morphine, and sublingual nitroglycerin (see image). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step? ECG: ST-elevation V2-V5
why_right: The ECG shows "ST-elevation V2-V5", an anterior STEMI, with 3 hours of continuous chest pain, so she needs urgent reperfusion. Primary PCI via urgent coronary angiography is the preferred strategy, and here it is the only safe one because she had an "ischemic stroke 1 month ago", which is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV magnesium treats torsades de pointes or hypomagnesemia; it has no role in STEMI reperfusion.
B. CT angiography is used for suspected aortic dissection or for low to intermediate risk chest pain; with clear ST elevation it delays reperfusion.
D. Thrombolysis is the alternative when primary PCI is not available in time, but ischemic stroke within the last 3 months is an absolute contraindication.
key_concept:
STEMI = reperfusion; primary PCI first, fibrinolysis only if PCI cannot be done in time and no contraindication.
  • V1 to V4: septal and anterior (LAD)
  • II, III, aVF: inferior (usually RCA)
  • Absolute contraindications to lysis: any prior intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke within 3 months, active bleeding, suspected aortic dissection
  • Initial ACS care: aspirin, nitrate, O2 if hypoxic, analgesia, ECG within 10 minutes
exam_pearl: Recent ischemic stroke turns "PCI or lysis" into PCI only.

stem: A Patient with Fatigue, Recurrent ureteric stones and bone pain Ca: 3.50 mmol Parathyroid adenoma: 2cm parathyroid adenoma What's Most Appropriate NEXT Step In Management?
why_right: This recall's key is calcitonin. The calcium is "3.50 mmol", a severe level, in a symptomatic patient (fatigue, bone pain, stones), so the source treats the immediate priority as lowering calcium quickly before definitive surgery. After IV saline, calcitonin has the fastest onset (hours), whereas bisphosphonates take a few days to act. Parathyroidectomy for the 2 cm adenoma is the definitive treatment once calcium is controlled.
why_wrong_block:
A. An IV bisphosphonate is also used in severe hypercalcemia (often together with calcitonin) but its effect starts after about 2 to 4 days, so it is not the fastest acting choice.
C. Increasing dietary calcium makes no sense in severe hypercalcemia; the usual advice is normal calcium intake and good hydration.
D. Parathyroidectomy is the definitive cure and is clearly indicated (symptomatic, stones, bone disease), but the source places acute control of severe calcium first.
key_concept:
Severe hypercalcemia: fluids, then calcium lowering drugs, then treat the cause.
  • Step 1: aggressive IV normal saline (loop diuretic only if fluid overloaded)
  • Step 2: calcitonin (fast, hours, short lived) plus IV bisphosphonate (slower, lasting)
  • Refractory or renal failure: denosumab or dialysis
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism: parathyroidectomy if symptomatic, stones, osteoporosis, age below 50 or calcium well above normal
  • Localize the adenoma (sestamibi) before surgery
exam_pearl: Mild or stable PHPT with surgical indication = parathyroidectomy; very high calcium = stabilize first (fluids, calcitonin).

stem: TLS patient with nausea, palpitations and muscle weakness, what’s causing it?
why_right: Tumor lysis releases intracellular potassium, and hyperkalemia is the TLS abnormality that kills through arrhythmia. The clue triad here, nausea, palpitations and muscle weakness, is the classic hyperkalemia picture: GI upset, cardiac irritability and flaccid weakness from depolarisation block. There are no cramps, tetany or paraesthesia that would point to calcium instead.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hypocalcemia does occur in TLS (phosphate binds calcium), but it presents with neuromuscular excitability: cramps, aches, perioral tingling, tetany, seizures. Weakness with palpitations fits potassium better.
C. Hyperuricemia is part of TLS, but it causes urate nephropathy and AKI, not palpitations or muscle weakness. It would be right if the question asked about the cause of renal failure in TLS.
D. Hypomagnesemia is not part of the TLS pattern (high K, high phosphate, high urate, low calcium). Think of it with diarrhoea, short bowel, TPN, alcohol or diuretics.
key_concept:
TLS = everything inside the cell goes UP, calcium goes DOWN.
  • Hyperkalemia: nausea, palpitations, weakness, arrhythmia (the lethal one)
  • Hyperphosphatemia: binds calcium, renal calcium phosphate deposition
  • Hypocalcemia: cramps, aches, tetany, seizures
  • Hyperuricemia: urate nephropathy, AKI
  • Prevention: hydration + allopurinol; rasburicase for established high urate
exam_pearl: Weakness + palpitations = potassium; cramps/aches/tetany = calcium. The companion card adds 'ache' and flips the key to hypocalcemia.

stem: TLS patient with nausea, palpitations and muscle weakness & Ache, what’s causing it?
why_right: In TLS, released phosphate binds calcium and drops serum calcium, and hypocalcemia produces neuromuscular irritability. The decisive added word in this version is 'Ache' (muscle aches/cramps), which together with weakness and palpitations (QT prolongation, arrhythmia) is the recall's cue for hypocalcemia. Hypocalcemia is also the classic 'associated' electrolyte abnormality asked about in TLS questions.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hyperkalemia is the most dangerous TLS abnormality and explains nausea, palpitations and weakness, but it does not cause muscle aches or cramps; it is the key in the sister card without 'ache'.
C. Hyperuricemia causes acute urate nephropathy and AKI rather than muscle symptoms; it would be right for a question about renal failure or allopurinol/rasburicase.
D. Hypomagnesemia can cause cramps and arrhythmia, but it is not part of the TLS pattern; think of it with diarrhoea, TPN, alcohol or diuretics.
key_concept:
TLS pattern: high K, high phosphate, high urate, LOW calcium.
  • Low calcium = phosphate binding calcium
  • Hypocalcemia: cramps, aches, perioral tingling, tetany, seizures, long QT
  • Hyperkalemia: weakness, palpitations, peaked T waves
  • Do not give calcium routinely for asymptomatic TLS hypocalcemia (worsens calcium phosphate deposition)
exam_pearl: Same stem as the hyperkalemia card; the single word 'ache' (cramps) is what moves the answer to hypocalcemia.

stem: elderly hypertensive man presents with acute onset of ataxia, ipsilateral facial sensory loss, dysphagia, Horner’s syndrome, and contralateral lower limb weakness. Which of the following arteries is most likely affected?
why_right: Ataxia, ipsilateral facial sensory loss, dysphagia and Horner's syndrome in an elderly hypertensive are the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, classically from PICA (or its parent vertebral artery) occlusion. Ipsilateral face plus contralateral body involvement (crossed signs) localises to the brainstem, and dysphagia/hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus) localises to the medulla rather than the pons.
why_wrong_block:
B. AICA (lateral pontine syndrome) also gives ataxia, Horner's and crossed sensory loss, but adds ipsilateral facial paralysis, hearing loss and vertigo; dysphagia from nucleus ambiguus points to the medulla, not the pons.
C. 'Anterior cerebellar' is not a standard vessel name; cerebellar supply is from PICA, AICA and the superior cerebellar artery, and a pure cerebellar infarct gives ataxia without Horner's, dysphagia or crossed facial sensory loss.
D. Basilar occlusion causes bilateral signs: quadriparesis, coma or locked-in syndrome, with ophthalmoplegia; it would be right for sudden bilateral weakness with reduced consciousness.
key_concept:
Posterior circulation localisation:
  • PICA / lateral medulla (Wallenberg): dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral Horner's and face pain/temp loss, contralateral body pain/temp loss, ataxia, vertigo
  • AICA / lateral pons: as above + facial palsy + deafness
  • Medial medulla (anterior spinal): contralateral hemiparesis, tongue deviates to lesion side
  • Basilar: bilateral signs, coma, locked-in
  • ACA: contralateral leg weakness; MCA: contralateral face/arm
exam_pearl: Classic Wallenberg gives contralateral body pain/temperature loss, not weakness; the 'lower limb weakness' in this recall is likely garbled, so anchor on dysphagia + Horner's + crossed facial sensory loss = PICA.

stem: pt with ST elevation and previous stroke Most appropriate management?
why_right: ST elevation means STEMI, and the preferred reperfusion is coronary angiography with primary PCI. The decisive clue is 'previous stroke': prior intracranial haemorrhage, or ischemic stroke within 3 months, is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis, so the catheter route is both first line and the only safe reperfusion option.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT angiography is not a STEMI treatment and only delays reperfusion; it would be right for suspected aortic dissection or PE, or as part of acute stroke workup.
C. Thrombolysis is second line, used only when timely PCI is unavailable, and prior stroke (any haemorrhagic, or ischemic within 3 months) contraindicates it because of intracranial bleeding risk.
key_concept:
STEMI: primary PCI first; fibrinolysis only if PCI not achievable in time and no contraindication.
  • Absolute: any prior ICH
  • Absolute: ischemic stroke within 3 months
  • Absolute: known AVM or intracranial tumour
  • Absolute: suspected aortic dissection
  • Absolute: active bleeding or bleeding diathesis
  • Absolute: significant head/facial trauma within 3 months
exam_pearl: Any STEMI stem with a bleeding or stroke history is steering you away from thrombolysis toward PCI.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for history of galactorrhea, worsening fatigue, malaise and irregular excessive menses for the last 5 months. She complains of headaches that occur about 2 to 3 times per week. Her physical examination is unremarkable. Pregnancy test was negative (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate management? Blood pressure 120/86 mmHg; Heart rate 62/min; Respiratory rate 13/min; BMI 28 kg/m2; Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone 16 (0.4 - 5.0 µU/mL); Thyroxine (T4 free serum) 9.2 (8.5 - 15.2 pmol/L); Prolactin 500 (< 652 pmol/L male, < 870 pmol/L female); Human chorionic gonadotropin 0.0 (< 5 mIU/mL)
OptD: Observation and retest thyroid function test in 6 months
why_right: Labs show TSH 16 with a normal free T4 (subclinical hypothyroidism) in a woman with fatigue, malaise, heavy irregular menses and galactorrhea, all explained by hypothyroidism. TSH above 10, especially when symptomatic, is an indication to begin levothyroxine. Prolactin (500) is within the female normal range, so the galactorrhea is TRH driven and will settle once the thyroid is treated.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cabergoline treats prolactinoma or significant hyperprolactinemia; here prolactin is normal and the cause is hypothyroidism, so a dopamine agonist treats nothing.
C. Pituitary MRI comes after confirming hyperprolactinemia not explained by pregnancy, drugs or hypothyroidism; with normal prolactin and a clear thyroid cause, imaging is not indicated (headaches alone do not justify it here).
D. Observation with repeat TFTs suits subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH below 10 and no symptoms; TSH 16 with symptoms needs treatment now.
key_concept:
Galactorrhea workup: pregnancy test, then TSH + prolactin, then pituitary MRI, then treat.
  • Primary hypothyroidism: high TRH stimulates prolactin, causing galactorrhea and menstrual disturbance
  • Subclinical hypothyroidism, TSH ≥10: start levothyroxine
  • TSH below 10, asymptomatic: observe and repeat TFTs
  • Prolactinoma: cabergoline first line; surgery for compressive symptoms or failure
exam_pearl: Always check TSH before blaming a prolactinoma; treating the thyroid fixes the galactorrhea.

stem: A 61-year-old woman is evaluated for a left pulmonary nodule that was discovered incidentally 2 months ago. She is currently asymptomatic and has not had shortness of breath, fever, chills, weight loss, or night sweats. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable, and she takes no medications. She never smoked. Examination revealed no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, and the lungs are clear to auscultation (see report). CT scan chest: Showed an 8 mm left lung nodule. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: An incidental 8 mm nodule in an asymptomatic never-smoker with no lymphadenopathy is low risk. A solid nodule of 8 mm or less is followed with surveillance CT rather than PET or biopsy, so observation with regular CT follow-up is the next step. PET/CT and tissue sampling are considered only above 8 mm.
why_wrong_block:
A. PET/CT scan: used for solid nodules larger than 8 mm (up to about 2 cm); at 8 mm and below PET is unreliable and not indicated.
B. Bronchoalveolar lavage: has no role in evaluating a small peripheral solitary nodule; used for diffuse infiltrates or suspected infection.
C. Transthoracic lung biopsy: invasive; reserved for larger (above 8 mm) suspicious or growing nodules, after PET/CT.
key_concept:
Solitary solid nodule by size (low-risk patient):
  • Small (current Fleischner <6 mm; older teaching ≤4 mm): no routine follow-up
  • Up to 8 mm (Fleischner 6 to 8 mm): surveillance CT, about 6 to 12 months
  • >8 mm: CT at 3 months, PET/CT or tissue sampling
  • Growing nodule: refer to thoracic surgery
  • Solid nodule stable for about 2 years: benign, stop follow-up
exam_pearl: Exactly 8 mm sits in the surveillance band; PET starts only above 8 mm.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with pain and swelling of the hands with early morning stiffness for 3 months. She has photosensitivity, hair loss, difficulty climbing stairs, and Raynaud's phenomenon. Examination reveals active arthritis at the second and third proximal interphalangeal joints, malar rash, and healed ulcers at the tip of the second finger. Proximal muscle strength is 3/5 (see lab results). Antinuclear antibody (ANA titer 1: 2540) Which of the following antibodies will most likely confirm the diagnosis?
why_right: She has lupus-like features (photosensitivity, hair loss, malar rash, arthritis) together with Raynaud, digital ulcers (scleroderma-like) and proximal weakness 3/5 (myositis), plus a very high-titre ANA. Overlapping features of SLE, systemic sclerosis and polymyositis define mixed connective tissue disease, which is confirmed by high-titre anti-U1 RNP.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anti-Smith is the most specific antibody for SLE alone, but SLE does not explain myositis plus Raynaud with digital ulcers as an overlap.
C. Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE and tracks disease activity and nephritis; it is typically absent in MCTD.
D. Anti-CCP confirms rheumatoid arthritis. Her arthritis is part of a multisystem connective tissue picture with rash, Raynaud and myositis.
key_concept:
Match the antibody to the disease.
  • Anti-U1 RNP: mixed connective tissue disease
  • Anti-Smith: most specific for SLE; anti-dsDNA: SLE activity, nephritis
  • Anti-histone: drug-induced lupus
  • Anti-centromere: limited SSc (CREST); anti-Scl-70: diffuse SSc
  • Anti-Jo-1: polymyositis with interstitial lung disease
  • Anti-CCP: rheumatoid arthritis
exam_pearl: Lupus features PLUS myositis PLUS Raynaud/digital ulcers = overlap (MCTD), so anti-RNP, not anti-Smith.

stem: A 75-year-old man with COPD presented with acute exacerbation due to super-added pneumonia. He was managed with IV fluids, antibiotics, nebulized salbutamol, and nasal oxygen at 4 L/min. A few hours later, he started to become drowsy (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
OptD: Increase the frequency of nebulized salbutamol
