why_right: A COPD patient on "nasal oxygen at 4 L/min" who becomes "drowsy" a few hours later has oxygen induced hypercapnia (CO2 narcosis): excess oxygen worsens V/Q mismatch and reduces ventilatory drive. The immediate step is to reduce inspired oxygen, using a Venturi mask titrated to SpO2 88 to 92%, then recheck the blood gas.
why_wrong_block:
A. NIV is the next step if hypercapnic acidosis persists after correcting oxygen and giving bronchodilators and steroids; it needs an alert, cooperative patient.
B. Ipratropium is part of exacerbation treatment but does not reverse CO2 retention caused by excess oxygen.
D. More salbutamol treats bronchospasm, not the CO2 narcosis driving the drowsiness.
key_concept:
COPD + oxygen + new drowsiness = CO2 retention: cut the FiO2 first.
  • Target SpO2 in COPD: 88 to 92% via Venturi mask
  • Bronchodilators: nebulized SABA + SAMA
  • Systemic steroid + antibiotics if infective
  • NIV: persistent hypercapnic acidosis despite medical therapy, alert patient
  • Intubation: unconscious, aspiration risk, failing NIV
exam_pearl: "Immediate" points to removing the cause (excess oxygen) before escalating to NIV.

stem: A 32-year-old man with HIV presents to the clinic for follow-up. He is generally doing well. However, Mantoux tuberculin test (PPD) after 48 hours is 6 mm. His chest radiography (CXR) is unremarkable. Which of the following is the best preventative measure for this patient?
OptD: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 9 months
why_right: In a person with HIV, a Mantoux induration of ≥5 mm is positive, so 6 mm means TB infection. A normal chest X-ray in a well patient means latent, not active, TB, so preventive therapy is needed; the classic regimen is isoniazid for 9 months with pyridoxine to prevent isoniazid neuropathy.
why_wrong_block:
A. 6 mm is positive in HIV (cut-off ≥5 mm), and HIV patients have a high risk of reactivation, so preventive treatment is mandatory. No treatment would be right only if induration were <5 mm.
C. Three months of isoniazid alone is too short; the valid 3-month regimens combine isoniazid with a rifamycin (rifapentine weekly or rifampin daily), not isoniazid alone.
D. Four-drug therapy is for active TB (symptoms, abnormal CXR, positive cultures); this patient has latent infection.
key_concept:
PPD cut-offs and latent TB treatment.
  • ≥5 mm: HIV, recent close contact, fibrotic CXR, immunosuppressed
  • ≥10 mm: healthcare workers, recent immigrants, IV drug users, high-risk settings
  • ≥15 mm: no risk factors
  • Latent TB: isoniazid + pyridoxine (6 to 9 months; 9 in HIV) or rifamycin-based short regimens
  • Active TB: RIPE four drugs
exam_pearl: Check the cut-off first: in HIV, 5 mm is already positive.

stem: A 29-year-old nurse is evaluated in the clinic for employment contract renewal. She is asymptomatic, and her clinical examination is unremarkable. Her laboratory tests are within normal range. Her skin purified protein derivative (PPD) test after 48 hours is 12 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptD: Isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol for 6 months
why_right: A nurse (healthcare worker, high-risk setting) has a PPD of 12 mm, which is positive at her 10 mm cutoff. She is asymptomatic with a normal examination, so this is latent TB, not active disease, and it needs preventive treatment to stop reactivation. Of the options, isoniazid 300 mg daily for 6 months is a recognised latent TB regimen (after a chest X-ray excludes active TB).
why_wrong_block:
A. No intervention is right only for a negative test (for example, under 10 mm in a healthcare worker without other risk); a positive PPD in a healthcare worker needs treatment.
B. Isoniazid alone for 3 months is not a recognised regimen; 3-month regimens combine isoniazid with rifampicin (or rifapentine).
D. A multidrug regimen is for active TB (symptoms, abnormal chest X-ray, positive sputum); she has latent infection only.
key_concept:
TST cutoffs and latent TB regimens
  • ≥5 mm: HIV, recent contacts, fibrotic CXR changes, transplant/immunosuppressed
  • ≥10 mm: healthcare workers, recent migrants from endemic areas, IV drug users, children <4 years
  • ≥15 mm: no risk factors
  • Regimens: isoniazid 6 or 9 months; shorter rifamycin-based options (rifampicin 4 months, isoniazid + rifampicin 3 months, weekly isoniazid + rifapentine 3 months) are now often preferred
  • Always exclude active TB (CXR) first
exam_pearl: The same 12 mm is negative in a person with no risk factors (needs ≥15 mm) but positive in a healthcare worker.

stem: A young man who is sexually active is evaluated in the clinic for clinical features that suggest gonorrhea. Which of the following tests is the most appropriate to establish the diagnosis?
why_right: Gonorrhea in a "sexually active" young man presents as urethritis, so the diagnostic specimen comes from the site of infection: a urethral swab for NAAT (or Gram stain and culture for sensitivities). Gram negative intracellular diplococci on a urethral smear support the diagnosis in symptomatic men.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood culture: only useful in disseminated gonococcal infection (fever, tenosynovitis, pustular skin lesions, septic arthritis), not localized urethritis.
B. Urinary culture: standard urine culture does not grow Neisseria gonorrhoeae; first-void urine is acceptable only for NAAT, not routine culture.
D. Vesicular rash swabs: for genital herpes (HSV PCR of vesicle fluid), which presents with painful vesicles or ulcers, not urethral discharge.
key_concept:
Gonococcal urethritis: sample the urethra.
  • Test of choice: NAAT on urethral swab or first-void urine
  • Urethral Gram stain: Gram negative intracellular diplococci
  • Culture: needed for antibiotic sensitivities
  • Disseminated disease: add blood and joint cultures
  • Always test for chlamydia too
exam_pearl: "Urine culture" is the trap: routine urine culture misses gonorrhea; only urine NAAT works.

stem: A 35-year-old woman who had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery 2 weeks ago presented to the Emergency Room complaining of chest pain for 1 day, associated with exertional shortness of breath, no cough, no fever, no orthopnea, and no PND. Examination revealed an ill-looking woman (see reports). Pulmonary function test: FEV1 90% (80%-120%) FVC 95% (80%-120%) TLC 95% (80%-120%) DLCO 40% (60%-120%) Which of the following is the most likely cause of her shortness of breath?
why_right: She is 2 weeks postpartum, a hypercoagulable state, with acute chest pain and exertional dyspnea but no cough, fever, orthopnea or PND. The PFTs show normal FEV1, FVC and TLC with an isolated low DLCO (40%): airways and lung volumes are normal but gas transfer is impaired, which points to a pulmonary vascular problem. This combination makes pulmonary embolism the most likely cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pneumonia: expect fever and productive cough with crackles or consolidation; both fever and cough are absent here.
B. Heart failure (including peripartum cardiomyopathy): expect orthopnea, PND, raised JVP, crackles and edema; she has no orthopnea or PND.
C. Acute bronchitis: productive cough and wheeze after a viral illness; she has no cough and her spirometry is normal.
key_concept:
Isolated low DLCO with normal spirometry and normal TLC = pulmonary vascular disease (PE, pulmonary hypertension).
  • Low FEV1/FVC + high TLC + low DLCO: emphysema
  • Low FEV1/FVC + normal DLCO: asthma or chronic bronchitis
  • Low TLC + low DLCO: interstitial lung disease
  • Low TLC + normal DLCO: extrapulmonary restriction (obesity, neuromuscular, chest wall)
  • Normal volumes + low DLCO: PE, pulmonary hypertension, anemia
exam_pearl: Postpartum + orthopnea, S3, raised JVP = peripartum cardiomyopathy; postpartum + clear history with isolated low DLCO = PE.

stem: A 69-year-old man complains of shortness of breath and weight loss for the last 6 months. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and no TB or HIV risk factors (see reports). Chest X-ray: A large left-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis: 1,500 mL of bloody fluid that is strongly exudative by Light's criteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 69-year-old, 40 pack-year smoker with 6 months of weight loss and a large bloody exudative effusion most likely has lung cancer (or pleural malignancy). The next step is contrast CT of the chest to show the underlying mass, nodes and pleural thickening and to plan an image-guided biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Empirical antibiotics suit a parapneumonic effusion with fever, cough and raised inflammatory markers, not a bloody effusion with months of weight loss.
C. Blind pleural biopsy has low yield; when malignancy is suspected, biopsy should be CT-guided or thoracoscopic after CT has mapped the pleura.
key_concept:
Pleural effusion work-up:
  • Step 1: diagnostic thoracentesis, apply Light's criteria
  • Transudate: treat the cause (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic)
  • Exudate unexplained: contrast CT chest
  • Suspected malignancy: CT-guided pleural biopsy or thoracoscopy
  • Bloody effusion: malignancy, trauma, PE, TB
exam_pearl: Smoker + weight loss + bloody exudate = malignancy until proven otherwise; image before you biopsy.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1304).

stem: A 55 year old non-smoker male present to the clinic, his blood pressure was 140/90 at multiple visits to the clinic. When measured at home it never exceeded 130/85. He is not known to have any disease, not on any medications. Many labs were given, all within normal range (kidney function, CBC, A1C). Lipid profile was not presented. What is his CVD risk?
why_right: Formal CVD risk scores (ASCVD/pooled cohort, Framingham, QRISK, SCORE) all require total and HDL cholesterol together with age, sex, BP and smoking. The stem stresses that the lipid profile was not presented, so his 10-year risk cannot be calculated and the answer is risk cannot be identified. His BP pattern (office 140/90, home never above 130/85) also suggests white coat hypertension rather than established hypertension.
why_wrong_block:
A. Low risk is tempting (non-smoker, normal labs), but a 55-year-old man cannot be labelled low risk without lipids; it would be right if a calculated score fell in the low band.
B. High risk is assigned without calculation only for established ASCVD, diabetes with organ damage, CKD, or very high LDL; he has none of these.
C. Intermediate risk is a calculated category from a scoring tool; it cannot be assigned without the cholesterol values the score requires.
key_concept:
CVD risk estimation needs: age, sex, smoking, systolic BP (treated or not), total and HDL cholesterol, diabetes status.
  • Automatically high risk: established ASCVD, diabetes with target organ damage, CKD, familial hypercholesterolaemia
  • Otherwise calculate the 10-year score
  • Missing lipids = risk cannot be calculated; order a lipid profile
  • Office high, home/ABPM normal = white coat hypertension
exam_pearl: When the stem pointedly says a required input is missing, the answer is 'cannot be determined', not a guess at the category.

stem: Very short case. A patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Laboratory results show: Blood glucose: 380 mg/dl, pH 7.15, Bicarbonate 15 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: The labs confirm DKA (glucose 380 mg/dl, pH 7.15, bicarbonate 15). The initial management is IV fluid resuscitation plus IV regular insulin infusion, after checking potassium is not low, because fluids correct the profound dehydration and fixed-rate IV insulin stops ketogenesis and closes the anion gap.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV bicarbonate is reserved for very severe acidosis (pH below 6.9); at pH 7.15 it adds no benefit and risks hypokalemia and paradoxical CNS acidosis.
B. Subcutaneous insulin is used once DKA has resolved (overlapping with the infusion before stopping it); absorption is unreliable in a dehydrated acidotic patient, so it is not the initial treatment here.
key_concept:
DKA ladder: fluids, potassium, insulin, find the trigger.
  • Fluids first: 0.9% saline bolus, then 0.45% saline
  • Check K: if below 3.3, replace before insulin
  • Regular insulin IV infusion 0.1 U/kg/hr
  • Add dextrose when glucose falls, continue insulin until acidosis resolves
  • Bicarbonate only if pH below 6.9
  • Switch to SC basal insulin with overlap once resolved
exam_pearl: If the options separate fluids from insulin, fluids alone come first; if potassium is low, potassium comes before insulin.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2536B).
Compiler note: Same question shown twice. Numbered 693: 'Typical case of DKA. What is the most appropriate initial management?' A. Sodium bicarbonate / B. Subcutaneous insulin / C. IV fluids and regular insulin (highlighted). The fuller 'Q:' version adds labs and also highlights C.

stem: A patient with cirrhosis due to Hepatitis C has a history of recurrent ascites despite repeated drainage. What is the best dietary advice?
OptA: Sodium restriction less than 2 g per day
OptB: Fluid restriction less than 2 L per day
why_right: Ascites in cirrhosis results from renal sodium retention driven by portal hypertension, so the cornerstone dietary measure is sodium restriction below 2 g per day, combined with diuretics (spironolactone ± furosemide). The clue recurrent ascites despite repeated drainage means the fluid keeps reaccumulating because salt intake is not controlled.
why_wrong_block:
B. Fluid restriction is not needed for ascites itself; it is used only when significant dilutional hyponatremia develops, since water follows sodium.
C. Protein should not be restricted in cirrhosis; these patients are often malnourished and need adequate protein, even with hepatic encephalopathy in current practice.
D. Fat restriction has no role in managing ascites; it does not affect sodium or fluid balance.
key_concept:
Ascites in cirrhosis, step by step:
  • Treat the cause (here HCV antivirals, alcohol abstinence when relevant)
  • Sodium restriction below 2 g/day
  • Spironolactone first, add furosemide
  • Fluid restriction only for significant hyponatremia
  • Large-volume paracentesis (with albumin) for tense or refractory ascites; TIPS if recurrent
exam_pearl: Ascites = restrict SALT, not water; water restriction is the answer only when the stem gives low serum sodium.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Ascites = salt restriction. Hepatic encephalopathy: avoid protein to excrete ammonia. Hepatitis/liver cirrhosis/autoimmune hepatitis without encephalopathy = fat.

stem: A patient with liver cirrhosis due to hepatitis C has esophageal varices and altered cognitive function (confused and lethargic) following attack of hematemesis. The patient is inquiring about which nutrient should be restricted?
why_right: This recall's key is proteins because the patient has developed hepatic encephalopathy (confused and lethargic) after a variceal bleed, and blood in the gut is a large protein load that colonic bacteria convert to ammonia. The traditional teaching is to reduce dietary protein to lower ammonia production; among these options it is the only nutrient linked to encephalopathy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fat restriction has no role in hepatic encephalopathy; fat is not a source of ammonia.
C. Carbohydrates are the main energy source and should be maintained to prevent catabolism, which itself increases ammonia from muscle breakdown.
D. Minerals and vitamins are often deficient in cirrhosis (zinc, thiamine, fat-soluble vitamins) and should be supplemented, not restricted.
key_concept:
Hepatic encephalopathy: find and treat the precipitant, then lower ammonia.
  • Precipitants: GI bleeding, infection/SBP, constipation, hypokalemia, dehydration, sedatives
  • Lactulose first line; add rifaximin for recurrence
  • Variceal bleed: octreotide, IV ceftriaxone, endoscopic banding
  • Nutrition: adequate protein and calories; vegetable/dairy protein better tolerated
exam_pearl: Exam keys protein restriction for encephalopathy, but ascites alone gets SALT restriction; do not mix the two cards.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Hepatic encephalopathy: avoid protein to excrete ammonia (compiler's note).

stem: 55-year-old man with liver cirrhosis on regular follow-up presents to the Emergency Room with a 2-day history of decreased level of consciousness and increased abdominal girth. Examination reveals an ill and cachectic patient with tense ascites and lower limb pitting edema bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: This recall's key is starting a diuretic combined with spironolactone. The patient has liver cirrhosis with ascites and bilateral pitting edema, and in cirrhotic ascites the aldosterone antagonist spironolactone is the diuretic backbone (secondary hyperaldosteronism drives sodium retention), usually paired with a loop diuretic. Sodium restriction plus spironolactone with furosemide is the standard medical regimen for cirrhotic fluid overload.
why_wrong_block:
A. Loop diuretic alone is the diuretic of choice in heart failure; in cirrhosis it is weak on its own because it does not block the aldosterone driven sodium retention, so it is added to spironolactone, not used instead of it.
C. TIPS is reserved for refractory ascites after diuretics and repeated paracentesis fail, and it worsens hepatic encephalopathy, which this patient with decreased level of consciousness may already have.
D. Therapeutic paracentesis gives quick relief of tense ascites but removes fluid without treating the ongoing sodium retention, so it must always be followed by diuretics; this recall keys the diuretic regimen itself (see concern).
key_concept:
Cirrhotic ascites ladder: treat cause → sodium restriction → diuretics → paracentesis → TIPS/transplant.
  • Spironolactone = diuretic of choice in cirrhosis
  • Furosemide = diuretic of choice in heart failure; added to spironolactone in cirrhosis
  • Tense or refractory ascites → therapeutic paracentesis
  • Refractory despite diuretics and paracentesis → TIPS
  • Confusion in cirrhosis → look for precipitants (SBP, GI bleed, infection)
exam_pearl: Cirrhosis: spironolactone first; heart failure: furosemide first. TIPS worsens encephalopathy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Embedded screenshot (0096) of the same question (options A-C) also gives Answer: B.

stem: pt with ascites best diuretics
key_concept:
Pick the diuretic by the cause of fluid overload.
  • Cirrhotic ascites: spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist) first
  • Heart failure congestion: furosemide (loop) first
  • Cirrhosis with edema or poor response: spironolactone plus furosemide
exam_pearl: "Ascites" in an exam stem usually means cirrhosis, which favours spironolactone; a heart failure stem favours frusemide.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler's Q: follow-up under 697; no option marked.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 60-year-old man is evaluated during a follow-up visit for management of newly diagnosed hypertension and diabetes mellitus started on metformin and gliclazide but not started on antihypertensive therapy. Physical examination is unremarkable (see lab results). Blood pressure 155/95 mmHg, Heart rate 80/min, BMI 32.5 kg/m2. BUN 5 (2.8-8.9 mmol/L); Creatinine 100 (44-115 µmol/L); Random Glucose 6 (3.9-5.5 mmol/L); HbA1c 6.9 (4.7-5.6 %); Urine Protein Present (absent); Urine Glucose Absent. Which of the following is the most appropriate antihypertensive treatment for this patient?
why_right: Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) is the first choice antihypertensive in a patient with diabetes and hypertension, especially with urine protein present. ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, lower intraglomerular pressure, reduce proteinuria and slow diabetic kidney disease. BP 155/95 with normal creatinine makes it safe to start.
why_wrong_block:
B. Atenolol is not first line in diabetic hypertension: it has no antiproteinuric effect and can mask hypoglycemia symptoms; it is used for specific indications such as angina or post MI.
C. Amlodipine lowers BP but does not reduce proteinuria; it is a good add-on or first choice in a non diabetic without proteinuria, not here.
D. Hydrochlorothiazide can worsen glucose and lipid control and lacks the renal protective effect; it is an add-on rather than the first agent when proteinuria is present.
key_concept:
Diabetes + hypertension (especially proteinuria): ACE inhibitor or ARB first.
  • Mechanism: efferent arteriole dilation → less albuminuria
  • ACE inhibitor not tolerated (cough) → ARB
  • Add-on: amlodipine or thiazide
  • Never combine ACE inhibitor with ARB
  • Check creatinine and potassium after starting
exam_pearl: Proteinuria in a diabetic flips any antihypertensive question to an ACE inhibitor or ARB.

stem: A 45-year-old woman, a smoker for 18 years, presented with exertional shortness of breath and a chronic cough for 5 months. She is also known to have long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. Chest examination revealed increased AP diameter with hyperresonance all over the chest and scattered crackles (see report). Pulmonary function test: Increase in total lung capacity and residual volume. FEV1 60% with no change post-bronchodilator. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Increase in total lung capacity and residual volume
why_right: "Increased AP diameter with hyperresonance" is the barrel chest of air trapping, and the PFT shows "increase in total lung capacity and residual volume" with FEV1 60% and "no change post-bronchodilator", an irreversible obstructive pattern. In a long-term smoker this is emphysema. The rheumatoid arthritis and crackles are distractors toward fibrosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lung fibrosis is restrictive: reduced TLC and RV, normal or high FEV1/FVC, with Velcro crackles and clubbing; it would be the answer in RA with that restrictive PFT.
C. Bronchiectasis causes copious purulent sputum and coarse crackles from dilated airways, usually after recurrent infection; it does not give hyperinflation with raised TLC as the main picture.
D. Allergic (hypersensitivity) pneumonitis follows antigen exposure and causes a restrictive or mixed pattern, not hyperinflation with increased TLC.
key_concept:
PFT pattern sorts obstructive from restrictive disease.
  • Obstructive: FEV1/FVC < 0.7, TLC and RV increased (air trapping)
  • Irreversible obstruction in a smoker: COPD (emphysema)
  • Reversible obstruction: asthma
  • Restrictive: TLC reduced, FEV1/FVC normal or high (fibrosis)
  • Emphysema keyword: barrel chest, hyperresonance
exam_pearl: RA in the stem pulls you to fibrosis, but raised TLC and RV with irreversible obstruction is emphysema; fibrosis lowers TLC.

stem: A 55-year-old man presented with a productive cough for 3 months. He had a similar attack of chronic cough for the previous 2 years. He smokes 1 pack/day for the last 15 years. Examination revealed an obese patient with scattered wheeze and crackles over the lungs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A smoker ("1 pack/day for 15 years") with a "productive cough for 3 months" and similar episodes in the "previous 2 years" meets the clinical definition of chronic bronchitis: productive cough for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years. Scattered wheeze and crackles reflect inflamed, mucus filled airways, and the obese habitus fits the classic "blue bloater".
why_wrong_block:
A. Bronchiectasis gives daily copious purulent sputum, hemoptysis, recurrent infections, coarse crackles and often clubbing, usually after TB or with cystic fibrosis; confirm by HRCT.
B. Asthma is episodic with variable, reversible airflow obstruction, typically in younger atopic patients; it does not explain a persistent productive cough recurring each year in a long term smoker.
C. Pulmonary fibrosis causes a dry cough, progressive dyspnea, fine end inspiratory (Velcro) crackles, clubbing and a restrictive pattern, not productive cough with wheeze.
key_concept:
Chronic bronchitis = productive cough ≥3 months in each of 2 consecutive years.
  • Smoker + productive cough + wheeze: chronic bronchitis (COPD)
  • Barrel chest + hyperresonance: emphysema
  • Copious sputum + hemoptysis + clubbing: bronchiectasis
  • Dry cough + Velcro crackles + clubbing: fibrosis
  • COPD diagnosis: spirometry; monitor with FEV1
exam_pearl: Productive + smoker + 3 months in 2 years = chronic bronchitis; dry + Velcro crackles = fibrosis.

stem: A 25-year-old woman with a known diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) presents to the clinic for follow-up. She is in remission and on teriflunomide. She reports transient worsening of her symptoms when exposed to heat. What is the explanation for her symptoms?
highlight_terms_source: transient worsening of her symptoms when exposed to heat
why_right: Uhthoff phenomenon is a transient worsening of existing MS symptoms when body temperature rises (hot weather, hot shower, exercise, fever). Heat slows conduction in demyelinated axons, so old deficits reappear and then resolve on cooling. The clues are in remission, transient worsening and the clear heat trigger.
why_wrong_block:
A. A relapse is a new or worsening deficit lasting more than 24 hours without fever or infection, often with new MRI lesions; here the symptoms are transient and heat triggered, so it is a pseudo-relapse.
B. Lhermitte sign is an electric shock sensation down the spine or limbs on neck flexion (cervical cord lesion), not heat triggered worsening.
D. ADEM is a monophasic post infectious or post vaccination demyelination, usually in children, with encephalopathy; it does not explain episodic heat sensitivity in known MS.
key_concept:
MS signs to tell apart:
  • Uhthoff: heat → transient worsening of old symptoms
  • Lhermitte: neck flexion → electric shock down spine
  • Relapse: new deficit > 24 h, no fever → IV methylprednisolone
  • Pseudo-relapse: heat or infection → treat trigger, no steroids
  • ADEM: monophasic, post infection, encephalopathy, usually children
exam_pearl: Transient + heat trigger = Uhthoff (pseudo-relapse), not a relapse needing steroids.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic with frequent heartburn. He had upper GI endoscopy and biopsy, which revealed Barrett's esophagus with low dysplasia. Which of the following is the best initial option in management?
why_right: Pantoprazole (a PPI) is the best initial step for Barrett's esophagus with low grade dysplasia. Acid suppression with a PPI is the foundation of all Barrett's management, combined with repeat endoscopic surveillance (about 6 months for low grade dysplasia). Resection is not indicated at this grade.
why_wrong_block:
A. Esophageal resection is for high grade dysplasia or invasive cancer not suitable for endoscopic therapy; low grade dysplasia does not justify surgery.
C. Ranitidine (H2 blocker) gives weaker acid suppression than a PPI; it may suit mild intermittent heartburn but not Barrett's.
D. Sucralfate is a mucosal protectant used mainly for ulcers or stress ulcer prophylaxis; it has no role in Barrett's.
key_concept:
Barrett's esophagus: PPI for all, then act on dysplasia grade.
  • No dysplasia: PPI + surveillance endoscopy
  • Low grade dysplasia (confirmed by a second pathologist): PPI + repeat endoscopy in about 6 months, or endoscopic ablation
  • High grade dysplasia or early cancer: endoscopic resection/ablation first; esophagectomy if not suitable
  • Barrett's → risk of adenocarcinoma of lower esophagus
exam_pearl: Low grade dysplasia = PPI + surveillance; high grade dysplasia = intervene.

stem: A woman presents with brief, jerky movements of one arm. There is no loss of consciousness, and the episode lasts only a few seconds. What is the most appropriate antiepileptic medication for management?
highlight_terms_source: brief, jerky movements of one arm
why_right: This recall's key is valproic acid, reading the brief, jerky movements lasting a few seconds with no loss of consciousness as myoclonic seizures. Valproate is the classic broad spectrum first line drug for myoclonic (and generalized) seizures, while narrow spectrum drugs can aggravate myoclonus.
why_wrong_block:
B. Lamotrigine is first line for focal seizures and an alternative in generalized epilepsy, but it can worsen myoclonic seizures, which is how this recall frames the jerks.
C. Ethosuximide treats only absence seizures (brief staring spells with impaired awareness, 3 Hz spike and wave); it does not control myoclonic or focal motor seizures.
D. Phenobarbital is mainly used in neonatal seizures and status epilepticus; sedation and cognitive effects make it a poor first choice here.
key_concept:
Match the antiepileptic to seizure type:
  • Myoclonic / generalized tonic-clonic: valproate (avoid in women of childbearing potential → levetiracetam or lamotrigine)
  • Absence: ethosuximide (or valproate)
  • Focal: lamotrigine or levetiracetam (carbamazepine alternative)
  • Neonatal: phenobarbital
  • Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen myoclonic and absence seizures
exam_pearl: Jerks with preserved consciousness = myoclonic → valproate; in a woman of childbearing age, valproate is avoided.

stem: 71 years old women present to ER complaining of fever disuria and suprabupic pain, His symptoms started 1 day ago but now after admission he developed confusion and disoriented to time place person and did not know where is she. Vital: High temperature, BP mentioned. Urinalysis shows: Positive nitrites, Positive leukocyte esterase, High Neutrophil (WBC). Investigations show: Calcium 1.97 mmol/L, Sodium 132 mmol/L, BUN 11 mmol/L, Random glucose 11 mmol. Brain MRI show: mild cortical atrophy. Which of the following will reverse his neurological symptoms?
why_right: Proper antibiotics reverse the confusion because this is delirium caused by a urinary tract infection in an elderly woman: fever, dysuria, suprapubic pain, positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase, then acute disorientation. Delirium resolves when its precipitant is treated, and the MRI shows only age related mild cortical atrophy, not a structural cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sodium 132 mmol/L is mild hyponatremia, which rarely causes confusion (usually below about 125 or when acute); it is not the driver here.
B. Calcium gluconate treats symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures, QT prolongation) or hyperkalemia; a mildly low total calcium in an unwell patient may simply reflect low albumin and does not explain the confusion.
C. IV fluids and monitoring are supportive and may be needed, but they do not remove the cause; without antibiotics the infection and delirium persist.
key_concept:
Elderly + acute confusion + infection = delirium: treat the precipitant.
  • Common causes: UTI, pneumonia, drugs, electrolytes, urinary retention, constipation
  • Fever + dysuria + nitrites/leukocyte esterase → UTI (send culture, start antibiotics)
  • Mild hyponatremia (130s) rarely explains confusion
  • Correct calcium for albumin before blaming it
exam_pearl: Delirium in the elderly is reversed by treating its cause; supportive fluids alone are not the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same question shown twice. Numbered 716: 'An elderly presents with fever, dysuria, and confusion. High BP Na 132 Ca ? Positive leukocytes in urine.' with options A. Correction of hyponatremia / B. Calcium gluconate / C. IV fluids / D. Proper antibiotics (highlighted). Fuller 'Q:' version used here, also highlighting D.

stem: A patient is known to have a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and has a cyanosis, irregular heart rhythm. S3 gallop. What is the most common cause of deterioration in this case?
OptC: Increase in the size of the PDA
why_right: Arrhythmia is the keyed cause of deterioration. A PDA is acyanotic, so cyanosis means long standing left to right shunt has caused pulmonary hypertension and shunt reversal (Eisenmenger), with right sided strain and dilated chambers. The irregular heart rhythm and S3 gallop point to atrial arrhythmia with heart failure, and arrhythmias are a leading cause of decompensation and death in Eisenmenger physiology.
why_wrong_block:
A. Infection (infective endarteritis, or chest infection) can complicate PDA and Eisenmenger syndrome, but the stem's clues are an irregular rhythm and S3, not fever or a new murmur.
C. The ductus does not enlarge with time; deterioration comes from pulmonary vascular disease, arrhythmia and ventricular failure, not a growing PDA.
key_concept:
Eisenmenger from a left to right shunt (VSD, ASD, PDA):
  • Shunt → pulmonary hypertension → shunt reversal → cyanosis
  • PDA reversal → differential cyanosis (lower limbs) and clubbing of toes
  • Deterioration: arrhythmia, heart failure, hemoptysis, stroke/brain abscess, endocarditis
  • Once Eisenmenger develops, closure of the defect is contraindicated
exam_pearl: Cyanosis in a known acyanotic lesion = Eisenmenger; irregular rhythm + S3 = arrhythmia driving decompensation.

stem: A 46-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room with back pain for 3 weeks associated with fever. She was sent home with NSAIDs and bed rest recommendations but returned after 2 days with the inability to move her legs. Examination revealed a febrile patient with tenderness in the mid-back and upper motor neuron signs in the lower limbs associated with weakness 3/5 (see lab results and report). MRI spine: Diffuse discitis in T6 vertebrae. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptD: Perform a bone marrow aspiration for culture
highlight_terms_source: back pain for 3 weeks associated with fever
why_right: Back pain with fever over 3 weeks points to an infective cause, and the MRI confirms discitis at T6, now complicated by cord involvement (UMN signs, weakness). In an endemic region such as Saudi Arabia, brucellosis is a leading cause of infective spondylodiscitis, and Brucella serology (titers by tube agglutination) is the initial, non invasive test that can establish the diagnosis quickly.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tuberculin (PPD) test: shows only TB exposure and cannot confirm active spinal TB; a negative or positive result does not settle the cause of the discitis.
C. Biopsy of T6 vertebrae: invasive; reserved for when serology and cultures are non diagnostic or TB or malignancy remains likely.
D. Perform a bone marrow aspiration for culture: invasive and not first line; it is used when serology and blood cultures fail to give a diagnosis.
key_concept:
Febrile back pain = infection until proven otherwise.
  • Brucella clues: raw milk or livestock contact, undulant fever, night sweats, sacroiliitis, spondylitis
  • Initial test: Brucella serology (tube agglutination)
  • Blood cultures are often negative in chronic disease
  • Biopsy or marrow culture only if non invasive tests are unhelpful
  • Spinal brucellosis needs prolonged combination antibiotics
exam_pearl: Choose the non invasive test first: serology before biopsy or marrow culture, even when TB is in the differential.

stem: A Female Patient Returned From A Trip To The Cold Mountains And Developed Chest Pain For The Past 3 Days. ECG Shows Diffuse ST-Segment Elevation. What Is The Most Likely Etiologic Agent?
highlight_terms_source: Chest Pain For The Past 3 Days
why_right: Chest pain for 3 days with diffuse ST-segment elevation is acute pericarditis (or myopericarditis), and the most common identified cause is viral, with Coxsackie B virus the classic agent. The trip to the cold mountains is a distractor; the key is diffuse rather than territorial ST elevation in a young patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. Echovirus is also an enterovirus that can cause pericarditis and myocarditis, but it is less common than Coxsackie B, so it is not the most likely agent.
B. Epstein-Barr virus causes infectious mononucleosis (fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly); cardiac involvement is rare.
C. Herpes simplex virus causes gingivostomatitis, genital lesions and encephalitis; it is not a typical cause of pericarditis.
key_concept:
Acute pericarditis: ≥2 of pleuritic positional chest pain, friction rub, diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, effusion.
  • Most common cause: idiopathic/viral (Coxsackie B)
  • Often follows a viral URTI by 1 to 2 weeks
  • ECG: diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, reciprocal changes only in aVR
  • Pain relieved by sitting forward
  • Treatment: NSAID + colchicine
exam_pearl: Diffuse ST elevation in a young patient = pericarditis, and the bug is Coxsackie B.

stem: 65-year-old man, a heavy smoker, known to have hypertension and COPD on Ventolin, Anoro Ellipta (Umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol), and lisinopril, presents with worsening shortness of breath for 4 months. There has been no change in his sputum amount or purulence, and he has had no fever, PND, or orthopnea. He was not admitted to the hospital for more than a year. Examination reveals decreased breath sounds without added sounds (see lab results and report). Chest CT 6 months ago: Diffuse emphysematous changes. Which of the following is the best intervention to improve his shortness of breath?
highlight_terms_source: worsening shortness of breath for 4 months
why_right: This heavy smoker with emphysema has worsening dyspnea for 4 months with no exacerbation features (no change in sputum, no fever, no admission for over a year) and no heart failure symptoms (no PND or orthopnea). He is already on maximal long-acting bronchodilators (Anoro Ellipta = LAMA + LABA), so further inhaler escalation will not help. The lab results are expected to show chronic hypoxemia meeting long-term oxygen criteria, so home oxygen is the intervention that corrects his hypoxemia and also improves survival in COPD.
why_wrong_block:
B. He already takes a LABA (vilanterol in Anoro Ellipta); adding another LABA duplicates the class and adds side effects without benefit.
C. Lung volume reduction surgery is for selected patients with upper lobe predominant emphysema and severe hyperinflation after pulmonary rehabilitation and smoking cessation; an active heavy smoker with diffuse emphysema is not a candidate.
D. Inhaled corticosteroids are added for frequent exacerbations (especially with raised blood eosinophils); he has had no exacerbations or admissions in over a year and ICS raise pneumonia risk.
key_concept:
COPD interventions that improve survival: smoking cessation, long-term oxygen, vaccination.
  • LTOT criteria (ABG when stable, on room air): PaO2 ≤55 mmHg or SaO2 ≤88%
  • Or PaO2 56 to 59 mmHg (SaO2 89%) with cor pulmonale/edema, pulmonary hypertension or polycythemia (HCT >55%)
  • Persistent dyspnea on LAMA/LABA → check oxygenation, refer for pulmonary rehab
  • ICS add-on: frequent exacerbations, high eosinophils
  • Smoking cessation: most important single factor; active smoking is a fire risk with home oxygen
exam_pearl: Already on LAMA + LABA with no exacerbations: the answer is not another inhaler; look at the ABG for LTOT criteria.

stem: Elderly man have progressive swallowing for solid and liquid Recently complain of epigastric pain and mild tenderness in examination The option
highlight_terms_source: progressive swallowing for solid and liquid
why_right: Upper GI endoscopy is needed because this elderly man has progressive dysphagia, a red flag symptom that mandates urgent endoscopy to exclude malignancy (esophageal or gastric cardia cancer). Endoscopy allows direct view and biopsy and also evaluates the epigastric pain.
why_wrong_block: A. H. pylori testing (urea breath or stool antigen) is the test and treat strategy for young dyspeptic patients without red flags; older age and progressive dysphagia require endoscopy instead.
key_concept:
Dyspepsia: red flags → endoscopy; no red flags → test for H. pylori.
  • Red flags: new symptoms at older age (above about 60), progressive dysphagia or odynophagia, weight loss, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding or anemia
  • Progressive dysphagia solids then liquids → think cancer
  • Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start → think achalasia (barium swallow, manometry), but endoscopy still first to exclude cancer
exam_pearl: Any dysphagia in an older patient = endoscopy first, never H. pylori testing.

stem: Patient with back pain, worsening at morning and improving within an hour after movement, positive schober test. What examination should be done next?
highlight_terms_source: improving within an hour after movement
why_right: Back pain that is worst in the morning, eases within an hour with movement, plus a positive Schober test (reduced lumbar flexion) is inflammatory back pain, i.e. ankylosing spondylitis. The next examination targets its commonest extra-articular feature, acute anterior uveitis (painful red eye, photophobia), so the eyes must be examined.
why_wrong_block:
B. A CNS exam for weakness looks for nerve root or cord compression, which suits mechanical or radicular back pain with neurological symptoms; inflammatory back pain that improves with exercise does not point there.
C. The cardiac lesion of ankylosing spondylitis is aortic regurgitation (aortitis) and conduction block, not mitral regurgitation.
key_concept:
Ankylosing spondylitis = inflammatory back pain + extra-articular 'A's.
  • Clues: young, morning stiffness improving with activity, worse with rest, positive Schober
  • Eye: anterior uveitis (most common extra-articular)
  • Heart: aortic regurgitation, heart block
  • Lung: apical fibrosis
  • Enthesitis: Achilles/heel pain
  • Dx: sacroiliitis on X-ray/MRI, HLA-B27; Rx: NSAID then TNF inhibitor
exam_pearl: Valve in AS is AORTIC, not mitral; the classic exam 'next exam' is the eye for uveitis.

stem: An 18-year-old girl brought by her parents to the Gastroenterology Clinic as they noticed her to have a fine tremor of both hands. Further examination showed jaundice and just palpable spleen (see lab results). Copper 0.8 (1.72-3.54 mmol/L Male, 1.72-3.76 mmol/L Female) Direct bilirubin 22.3 (1.5-6.5) Total bilirubin 38.2 (3.5-16.5) Aspartate aminotransferase 243 (12-40 IU/L) Alanine aminotransferase 165 (5-40 IU/L) Albumin 23 (34-56 g/L) Total Proteins 46 (60-84) Serum ceruloplasmin Low 24 hours urine copper High Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
why_right: A young patient (18 years) with tremor (extrapyramidal), jaundice, splenomegaly and low albumin, plus low ceruloplasmin, low total serum copper and high 24 h urine copper, has Wilson disease. Treatment is copper chelation, and D-penicillamine is the classic chelator.
why_wrong_block:
A. Corticosteroids treat autoimmune hepatitis (high IgG, autoantibodies); they do nothing for copper overload.
C. Desferrioxamine chelates iron, used in transfusional iron overload or hemochromatosis when venesection is not possible, not copper.
D. Ursodeoxycholic acid is for cholestatic disease such as primary biliary cholangitis; it does not remove copper.
key_concept:
Wilson disease = copper accumulation in liver, brain, eye, kidney.
  • Young + liver disease + neuro/psychiatric signs
  • Eye: Kayser-Fleischer ring
  • Labs: LOW ceruloplasmin, LOW total copper, HIGH free copper, HIGH urine copper
  • Rx: chelation (D-penicillamine; trientine alternative), zinc to block absorption
  • Iron overload instead: desferrioxamine
exam_pearl: Low TOTAL serum copper does not exclude Wilson: it is low because ceruloplasmin is low; free copper and urine copper are high.

stem: Patient underwent bone marrow transplantation due to SCD, developed febrile neutropenia and has pneumonia, she was given Ceftazidime and shows no improvement,in first week what to add?
why_right: This is febrile neutropenia after BMT with a documented pneumonia and no improvement on ceftazidime, still within the first week. Pneumonia (and sepsis, line or skin infection, MRSA) is an indication to add vancomycin for gram-positive cover, which ceftazidime lacks; antifungals are added later if fever persists beyond about 4 to 7 days.
why_wrong_block:
B. Tazocin is an alternative first-line anti-pseudomonal agent; swapping one gram-negative beta-lactam for another does not fill the gram-positive gap.
C. Ceftriaxone has no anti-pseudomonal activity, so it is a step down from ceftazidime in a neutropenic patient; it suits community-acquired pneumonia or meningitis.
D. Amphotericin B (empirical antifungal) is added when fever persists after about 4 to 7 days of broad antibiotics or when a fungal infection is shown; the stem specifies the first week.
key_concept:
Febrile neutropenia ladder:
  • Start: anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (meropenem, Tazocin, cefepime)
  • ADD vancomycin: pneumonia, sepsis/shock, line infection, skin/soft tissue infection, MRSA
  • ADD antifungal: fever persisting beyond about 4 to 7 days
  • Ceftriaxone is never adequate empiric cover in neutropenia
exam_pearl: Pneumonia or hemodynamic instability early = vancomycin; persistent fever late (after ~4 to 7 days) = antifungal.

stem: A Sickle cell disease patient who underwent bone marrow transplant. He got a fever 1 day after the procedure. He was started on ceftazidime but did not improve after 72 hours. There was no pneumonia or hypotension. What to add ?
why_right: Persistent fever on ceftazidime in a post-BMT neutropenic patient with no pneumonia, no hypotension (and, in the sister variant, no line or skin/mucosal lesions) means none of the indications for vancomycin are present. Fever that persists despite broad antibiotics in profound neutropenia raises invasive fungal infection, so an antifungal such as voriconazole (mould-active, first line for aspergillosis) is the keyed addition.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ceftriaxone lacks anti-pseudomonal cover, so adding or switching to it adds nothing to ceftazidime in neutropenia.
C. Sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) is used for Pneumocystis prophylaxis or treatment, not for unexplained persistent neutropenic fever.
D. Vancomycin is added only for specific indications (pneumonia, hypotension/sepsis, central line or skin infection, MRSA); the stem deliberately excludes these.
key_concept:
Persistent neutropenic fever: decide by the indication.
  • Pneumonia, shock, line or skin infection, MRSA: add vancomycin
  • None of these + fever persisting on antibiotics: add antifungal
  • Mould cover / aspergillosis: voriconazole
  • Empirical alternatives: echinocandin (caspofungin) or liposomal amphotericin
exam_pearl: Same BMT stem flips: WITH pneumonia = vancomycin, explicitly WITHOUT pneumonia/hypotension = antifungal.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant in same block: 'Patient underwent BMT due to SCD, febrile neutropenia, given Ceftazidime, no improvement after 72 hours (No Pneumonia, No Hypotension, No Central Line, No Skin/Mucus Ulcerations)' with options Vancomycin / Tazocin / Ceftriaxone / Voriconazole; Voriconazole highlighted.

stem: patient with acute leukemia recently underwent allogenic bone marrow transplantation. After 2 weeks, she was neutropenic and developed a fever and cough. She was diagnosed with invasive aspergillosis based on radiological and microbiological assessment. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
why_right: A neutropenic patient early after allogeneic bone marrow transplantation is at high risk of invasive mould infection, and here invasive aspergillosis is already confirmed. Aspergillus is a fungus, and voriconazole is the first line treatment for invasive aspergillosis; it is also the only antifungal among the options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rifampicin: an antimycobacterial antibiotic used in TB and brucellosis; it has no antifungal activity.
B. Valaciclovir: an antiviral for herpes simplex and varicella zoster infections; no activity against Aspergillus.
C. Tigecycline: a broad spectrum antibacterial (glycylcycline) for resistant bacteria; it does not treat fungal infection.
key_concept:
Match the drug class to the organism.
  • Invasive aspergillosis: voriconazole first line
  • Mucormycosis: amphotericin B
  • Herpes viruses: aciclovir or valaciclovir
  • Mycobacteria: rifampicin based regimens
  • Risk factors for invasive mould: prolonged neutropenia, stem cell transplant, high dose steroids
exam_pearl: Do not confuse aspergillosis with mucormycosis: voriconazole covers Aspergillus but not Mucor, which needs amphotericin B.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Shown as a 'Q:' variant within block 776.

stem: Patient underwent bone marrow transplantation due to SCD, developed febrile neutropenia and has [NO] Pneumonia , she was given Ceftazidime and shows no improvement, what to add?
why_right: This recall's key is vancomycin: a post-BMT neutropenic patient on ceftazidime who is not improving. Ceftazidime has weak gram-positive activity (viridans streptococci from mucositis, staphylococci from lines), and vancomycin is the only option that adds gram-positive and MRSA cover; no antifungal is offered here.
why_wrong_block:
B. Tazocin is an alternative first-line anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam; it does not add meaningful new cover over ceftazidime for a non-responder.
C. Ceftriaxone has no anti-pseudomonal activity, so it is a downgrade in a neutropenic patient.
D. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is for Pneumocystis prophylaxis or treatment, not empirical escalation for neutropenic fever.
key_concept:
Escalation in febrile neutropenia:
  • Base: anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam
  • Vancomycin: pneumonia, sepsis/hypotension, line or skin infection, mucositis, MRSA
  • Antifungal: fever persisting after about 4 to 7 days
  • If the options include an antifungal and the stem excludes vancomycin triggers, pick the antifungal
exam_pearl: Check the options: if an antifungal is listed and pneumonia/hypotension/line infection are explicitly absent, the sister variant keys voriconazole.

stem: Ascitis treated by sparonolactone with no improvment , managment ?
key_concept:
Cirrhotic ascites ladder.
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Therapeutic paracentesis.
  • 1: treat cause, sodium restriction
  • 2: spironolactone (add furosemide, titrate)
  • 3: large/tense or diuretic-resistant: therapeutic paracentesis + albumin
  • 4: recurrent need for paracentesis: TIPS (or liver transplant referral)
  • Fever/abdominal pain: diagnostic tap for SBP first
exam_pearl: TIPS only after repeated paracentesis fails or is needed too often; encephalopathy argues against TIPS.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 60-year-old man with liver cirrhosis presents to the Emergency Room with increasing ascites. He has no history of fever or decreased level of consciousness. His medications include spironolactone 50 mg/day and furosemide 40 mg/day. His physical examination confirms the presence of large ascites (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: This cirrhotic patient has large ascites despite spironolactone and furosemide, with no fever (SBP less likely) and no decreased consciousness (no encephalopathy). Large (tense) or diuretic resistant ascites is treated with therapeutic large volume paracentesis, with IV albumin given when large volumes are removed.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV diuretics have no role in cirrhotic ascites and risk renal impairment and electrolyte disturbance.
C. Raising the oral diuretic dose suits moderate ascites, but it will not relieve large ascites promptly; when diuretics are escalated, spironolactone and furosemide are increased together in a fixed ratio rather than furosemide alone.
D. TIPS is for refractory ascites needing frequent repeated large volume paracentesis, not the next step at this presentation.
key_concept:
Cirrhotic ascites ladder:
  • Treat the cause; sodium restriction
  • Diuretics: spironolactone (drug of choice) with or without furosemide
  • Large/tense or refractory: therapeutic large volume paracentesis + IV albumin
  • Repeated paracentesis needed: TIPS, consider transplant
  • Fever or abdominal pain: diagnostic tap for SBP (neutrophils >250)
exam_pearl: Fever or abdominal tenderness changes the answer to diagnostic paracentesis and IV antibiotics for SBP; its absence here keeps it therapeutic.

stem: Watary diarrhea
key_concept:
Diarrhea pattern decides the organism:
  • Acute vomiting-predominant outbreak: norovirus
  • Chronic watery + bloating + weight loss: Giardia
  • Bloody + fever + seizure in child: Shigella
  • Traveler's watery diarrhea soon after travel: E. coli (ETEC)
  • Rice-water, huge volume: Vibrio cholerae
  • Vomiting a few hours after a meal: S. aureus toxin
exam_pearl: Watery + weight loss + chronic = Giardia; blood and mucus rules out Giardia and norovirus.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 40-year-old woman is under treatment for a recurrent helicobacter-associated duodenal ulcer. She noticed that her stool is turned non-tarry black (see lab result). What drug is likely to be the cause of the black stools?
why_right: She is on treatment for recurrent H. pylori ulcer, which means bismuth quadruple therapy. Bismuth reacts with sulfide in the gut to form black bismuth sulfide, giving non-tarry black stool (and sometimes black tongue) with normal hemodynamics and hemoglobin, unlike melena.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ranitidine (H2 blocker) does not discolor stool.
B. Pantoprazole (PPI) does not cause black stool; it is the acid suppressant backbone of eradication regimens.
D. Aluminium hydroxide causes constipation (magnesium antacids cause diarrhea), not black stool.
key_concept:
Black stool: melena or drug?
  • Melena: tarry, sticky, foul, may drop Hb or cause tachycardia
  • Non-tarry black with stable vitals/Hb: bismuth or oral iron
  • Bismuth quadruple: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole (used for recurrence/failure)
  • Aluminium antacid: constipation
exam_pearl: 'Non-tarry' and normal Hb are the clues: harmless bismuth effect, not a rebleed.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant in same block: 32-year-old female on treatment of H.pylori, stool became dark (options Aluminum hydroxide / Bismuth subsalicylate / Ranitidine / PPI); Bismuth subsalicylate highlighted.

stem: patient is diagnosed with celiac disease. Which of the following foods should be avoided?
why_right: Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten, and the treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet. Wheat is the main gluten-containing grain, together with barley and rye.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rice is naturally gluten free and is a safe staple in celiac disease.
B. Maize (corn) is gluten free and safe.
C. Potatoes are gluten free and safe.
key_concept:
Gluten-free diet: avoid BRW (Barley, Rye, Wheat).
  • Safe: rice, maize/corn, potatoes
  • Oats: often contaminated with gluten, caution
  • Screen: IgA tTG; confirm: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy)
  • Associations: type 1 DM, dermatitis herpetiformis
exam_pearl: Variant keys barley instead of wheat: any of barley, rye or wheat is the one to avoid.

stem: 35 years old women known case of rheumatic heart disease, she had prosthetic valve replacement 3 years ago, she want to do dental operation. What is the appropriate prophylactic antibiotic?
why_right: A prosthetic valve is a high-risk cardiac condition and a dental operation is a high-risk procedure, so endocarditis prophylaxis is indicated. The standard regimen is a single oral dose of amoxicillin before the procedure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ampicillin IV/IM is the alternative only when the patient cannot take oral medication; oral amoxicillin is first choice.
C. Clindamycin was the old option for penicillin allergy and is no longer recommended by recent AHA guidance; no allergy is mentioned here.
D. Ceftriaxone IV/IM is a parenteral alternative for patients unable to take oral drugs, not the first-line choice.
key_concept:
IE prophylaxis needs BOTH a high-risk heart AND a high-risk procedure.
  • High-risk heart: prosthetic valve or prosthetic repair material, prior IE, certain congenital heart disease, transplant valvulopathy
  • High-risk procedure: dental work manipulating gingiva/periapical region or perforating mucosa
  • Drug: oral amoxicillin, single dose before
  • Cannot take oral: ampicillin or ceftriaxone IV/IM
  • Not needed: GI/GU procedures, hernia repair, rheumatic disease without prosthesis
exam_pearl: Prosthetic valve but non-dental surgery (e.g. hernia repair) = no IE prophylaxis; prophylaxis is a single pre-procedure dose, not before and after.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant in same block: 'Patient with mechanical valve/rheumatic heart disease undergoing dental procedure. Prophylaxis?' (Erythromycin 300mg or azythro? / Amoxicillin before and after procedure / No treatment); 'Amoxicillin before and after procedure' highlighted.

stem: A 53 yo man post angioplasty after MI 3 monthes ago now complaint on excercise and healthy life style presented to the opd His labs cholesterol was 5.3 and his blood pressure is 139/75 What is the appropriate counseling
highlight_terms_source: post angioplasty after MI 3 monthes ago
why_right: After an MI (here post angioplasty, MI 3 months ago) the patient has established coronary disease, so a lipid lowering drug (high intensity statin) is indicated for secondary prevention regardless of the baseline cholesterol. A total cholesterol of 5.3 mmol/L implies an LDL well above secondary prevention targets, and lifestyle alone will not reach them. That is why the counseling is to start lipid lowering medication on top of his exercise and diet.
why_wrong_block:
A. Annual cholesterol checks are a monitoring step for low risk primary prevention; a post MI patient needs treatment now, not surveillance.
B. Continuing exercise and diet is correct but insufficient on its own; after MI, lifestyle is always combined with statin therapy.
D. BP 139/75 is only borderline (post MI targets are lower, around 130/80), so the first step is lifestyle and repeat readings; an antihypertensive is added if it stays above target, whereas the statin is mandatory after MI.
key_concept:
Established ASCVD (MI, stent, stroke) = statin for life, whatever the cholesterol.
  • Secondary prevention: high intensity statin (e.g. atorvastatin 80) plus lifestyle
  • Primary prevention: risk score decides; lifestyle first if low risk
  • Post MI bundle: antiplatelet, statin, beta blocker, ACE inhibitor, cardiac rehab
  • Lifestyle alone is never the answer after an MI
exam_pearl: "Already on diet and exercise" is the distractor: after an MI, the statin is started even if the cholesterol looks only mildly raised.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant in same block: 'Patient with MI 3 month ago. Medically free, on diet and exercise, Bp 136/86, Cholesterol 5.6' (Anti hypertensive / Lipid lowering agent / Continue with exercise and diet); 'Lipid lowering agent' highlighted.

stem: 50 yo male veterinarian complaining of right sacro-iliac pain and fever for 2 monthes. Associated with back pain He also appears agitated, behavioral changes…. It was along long question the labs were HB 10 Low PLT What is the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: right sacro-iliac pain and fever for 2 monthes
why_right: A veterinarian (animal exposure) with fever for 2 months, sacroiliac and back pain, and behavioral change fits brucellosis: a zoonosis with subacute fever, musculoskeletal involvement (sacroiliitis, spondylitis) and possible neurobrucellosis. Anemia and low platelets reflect marrow and reticuloendothelial involvement, which is typical. The occupational exposure is the decisive clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. TB can cause chronic fever and spinal disease (Pott's), but it favours the thoracolumbar spine rather than the sacroiliac joint and has no link to animal work; consider it with cough, weight loss or TB contact.
B. Syphilis can cause neuropsychiatric change (neurosyphilis), but not prolonged fever with sacroiliitis; it would fit a sexual history, rash or chancre.
D. Toxoplasmosis (cat or undercooked meat exposure) causes lymphadenopathy or, in immunocompromised patients, brain abscesses; it does not cause sacroiliitis.
key_concept:
Animal contact or raw milk + prolonged fever + back/sacroiliac pain = brucellosis.
  • Organism: Gram negative coccobacillus
  • Features: undulant fever, sweats, arthralgia, sacroiliitis, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias
  • Neurobrucellosis: behavioral change, meningitis
  • Initial test: serology (tube agglutination); blood culture confirms
  • Treatment: doxycycline plus rifampicin (or plus an aminoglycoside)
exam_pearl: Sacroiliitis plus fever in a Saudi exam stem points to brucellosis first; TB spine favours the thoracic vertebrae.

stem: Known htn patient presented to the clinic after failed to reach target blood pressure. He is on amlodipine and losartan. His cbc and kidney function are normal. What to add
highlight_terms_source: failed to reach target blood pressure
why_right: He is already on an ARB (losartan) plus a calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) and is not at target, with normal kidney function. The standard third step is A + C + D: add a thiazide or thiazide like diuretic (e.g. indapamide). Normal renal function means a thiazide will still work.
why_wrong_block:
A. An ACE inhibitor duplicates the ARB he already takes; combining ACE inhibitor with ARB raises the risk of hyperkalemia and AKI and is avoided.
B. An alpha blocker is a fourth line (resistant hypertension) option, or chosen first when BPH symptoms coexist; it comes after the diuretic.
D. A beta blocker is reserved for a compelling indication (angina, post MI, heart failure, rate control) or later steps; it is not the standard third drug.
key_concept:
Hypertension ladder: A (ACEi or ARB) or C, then A + C, then A + C + D.
  • Step 3 = add thiazide like diuretic (indapamide, chlorthalidone)
  • Step 4 (resistant): spironolactone if K low or normal; else alpha or beta blocker
  • Never combine ACE inhibitor and ARB
  • Severe renal impairment: thiazides lose effect, use a loop diuretic
exam_pearl: Ask what class is missing from A + C + D; if renal function were poor, the diuretic would be a loop instead of a thiazide.
